p.seg: The foremost of the Southern Mountains is called Què Shān.
Its foremost peak is named Zhāoyáo Zhī Shān,
which overlooks the Western Sea,
abounds in cinnamon trees,
and is rich in metals and jade.
There is a plant here,
shaped like chives but with blue flowers,
called Zhùyú,
and eating it prevents hunger.
There is a tree here,
resembling the paper mulberry but with black veins,
Its flowers shine in all directions,
its name is Mígǔ,
and wearing it prevents one from getting lost.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a macaque with white ears,
it crawls like an animal but walks like a human,
its name is Xīngxīng,
and eating it makes one good at running.
The Lìjǐ waters originate here,
flow westward into the sea,
and in them are many Yùpèi,
wearing which prevents abdominal ailments.
Another three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Tángtíng,
with many persimmon trees,
many white apes,
much crystal,
and much gold.
Further east three hundred eighty li,
lies Jíyì Mountain,
where many strange beasts dwell,
the waters abound with strange fish,
there is much white jade,
many venomous reptiles,
numerous strange snakes,
many peculiar trees,
and it is impossible to ascend.
Another three hundred seventy li to the east,
there is a mountain called Niǔyángzhīshān,
on its sunny side there is much red gold,
on its shady side much white gold.
There is a beast here,
its form like a horse with a white head,
its stripes like a tiger with a red tail,
its call like a song,
its name is Lùshǔ,
Wearing it is beneficial for descendants.
Guài Shuǐ originates from there,
and flows eastward into Xiàn Yì Zhī Shuǐ.
In it, there are many xuán guī,
which look like turtles but have bird heads and snake tails,
their name is xuán guī,
their sound is like splitting wood,
wearing it prevents deafness,
and it can be used to treat foot ailments.
Three hundred li further east is called Zhī Shān,
with abundant water,
but no grass or trees.
There is a fish here,
whose shape resembles an ox,
dwelling on hills,
with a snake's tail and wings,
its feathers located below the ribs,
its call like that of a liú niú,
its name is Lù,
which dies in winter and comes to life in summer,
and eating it prevents swelling diseases.
Another four hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Chǎnyuán Zhī Shān.
It has abundant water,
but no grasses or trees,
and it is impossible to climb.
There is a beast there,
whose form is like a wildcat but has a mane,
named Lèi.
It possesses both male and female organs,
and those who eat it will not feel jealousy.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Jī Shān.
Its southern side abounds with jade,
while its northern side has many strange trees.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a sheep,
with nine tails and four ears,
and its eyes are on its back.
Its name is Bó Tuó.
Wearing it makes one fearless.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a chicken but with three heads and six eyes,
six legs and three wings,
its name is Chǎngfū,
and eating it prevents sleep.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Qīngqiū,
on its sunny side there is much jade,
on its shady side much green cinnabar.
There is a beast here,
its form like a fox with nine tails,
its cry like that of an infant,
and it can eat humans.
Eating it prevents one from being bewitched.
There is a bird here,
its form like a turtledove,
its call sounds like scolding,
named Guànguàn,
wearing it prevents confusion.
The Yīng River flows out from here,
running southward into the Jíyì Marsh.
In it dwell many chìrú,
which have the form of fish with human faces,
and their calls sound like those of mandarin ducks.
Eating them prevents skin diseases.
Three hundred and fifty li further east,
there is a mountain called Jīwěi,
its tail crouches by the Eastern Sea,
with much sand and stone.
The Fāngshuǐ River originates here,
flowing south into the Yù,
and within it, there is an abundance of white jade.
All the mountains of the Que range,
from Mount Zhāoyáo,
to Mount Jīwěi,
total ten mountains,
spanning 2,950 li.
Their deities all have bird bodies and dragon heads.
The ritual for sacrificing to it:
the fur is buried with one zhang jade,
the sacrificial grain is glutinous rice,
one bi disc,
rice,
and white sedge grass is used as the mat.
The beginning of the Second Southern Classic,
is called Jù Shān,
to the west it borders Liú Huáng,
to the north it overlooks Zhū Pí,
to the east it overlooks Cháng Yòu.
Yīng Shuǐ originates here,
flowing southwest into Chì Shuǐ,
in which there is much white jade,
and much cinnabar sand.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a pig,
with spurs,
its call resembling a dog's bark,
named Lílì,
whose appearance foretells much earthwork in the county.
There is a bird here,
shaped like an owl with human hands,
its sound like a numbness,
named Zhū,
its cry is its own name,
whose appearance foretells many exiled scholars in the county.
Four hundred fifty li to the southeast,
there is Mount Chángyòu,
devoid of grass and trees,
with abundant water.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a macaque but with four ears,
named Chángyòu,
its call sounds like chanting,
and when it appears, the commanderies and counties suffer great floods.
Three hundred and forty li further east,
there is a mountain called Yáoguāngzhīshān.
On its sunny side, there is much jade,
and on its shady side, much gold.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a human but with a boar's bristles,
that dwells in caves and hibernates in winter.
Its name is Huáhuái,
and its call sounds like chopping wood.
When it appears, the county will face great labor conscription.
Three hundred and fifty li further east,
there is Yǔ Shān.
At its foot, there is much water,
and on its summit, frequent rain.
It has no grasses or trees,
but many venomous snakes.
Further east three hundred seventy li,
there is a mountain called Qūfùzhīshān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in metal and jade.
Further east four hundred li,
there is a mountain called Jūyúzhīshān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in metal and jade.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Fúyù,
to the north of which one can see Jùqū,
and to the east, Zhūpí.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a tiger with an ox's tail,
its cry like a barking dog,
named Zhì,
which eats people.
The Tiáo River originates from its northern side,
flowing north into Jùqū,
where many Cí fish are found.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Chéngshān,
which is square in shape with three tiers,
rich in metal and jade on its summit,
and abundant in green mineral pigments at its base.
The Shuōshuǐ River originates here,
flowing southward into the Hūsháo River,
and contains much gold within its waters.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Huìjī,
square in shape,
with abundant metal and jade on its summit,
and plentiful veined stones at its base.
The Sháo River originates here,
flowing southward into the Jú River.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Yí Shān,
with no grass or trees,
abundant in sand and stones.
The Jù Shuǐ originates from here,
and flows southward into Liè Tú.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is Mount Púgōu.
On its summit, there is abundant metal and jade,
at its base, there is much grass and trees,
but no birds or beasts,
and no water.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Xiányīn,
with no grass or trees,
and no water.
Another four hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Xún Shān.
On its southern side, there is much metal,
and on its northern side, much jade.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a sheep but without a mouth,
that cannot be killed,
and its name is Huàn.
The Xún River flows from here,
and runs southward into the È Swamp,
where there are many purple snails.
Another four hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Hūsháo,
on which there are many catalpa and nanmu trees,
and below which there are many brambles and wolfberries.
The Pāng River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into the sea.
Again east five hundred li,
there is a mountain called Qūwúzhīshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
abundant in sand and stones.
Lùshuǐ originates from it,
and flows south to pour into Pāngshuǐ.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Lùwúzhīshān.
It has no grass or trees on its summit,
but is rich in metals and stones.
The Zégèng River originates from here,
flowing southward into the Pāng River.
There is a beast dwelling there,
named Gǔdiāo,
which resembles an eagle but has horns,
and its cry sounds like that of an infant.
It is a man-eater.
Five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Qīwúzhī Shān.
It has no grass or trees,
but abounds in bo stones,
and has no jade.
It is situated by the sea,
and to the east, one gazes upon hills,
where the light appears and disappears,
for this is where the sun rests.
The beginning of the "Second Southern Classic" records,
from Jù Shān to Qīwú Zhī Shān,
a total of seventeen mountains,
spanning seven thousand two hundred lǐ.
The deities here all have dragon bodies and bird heads.
For their sacrifices:
the sacrificial animal is buried with a jade disc,
and the offering grain is glutinous rice.
The first of the Southern Third Range,
is called Tiānyú Mountain,
with abundant water below it,
making it impossible to ascend.
Five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Dǎoguò,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and below it there are many rhinoceroses,
wild buffaloes, and many elephants.
There is a bird there,
whose form resembles a Jiao,
but it has a white head, three feet, and a human face,
its name is Qúrú,
and its call is the sound of its own name.
The Yǐn River emerges here,
and flows southward into the sea.
Within it dwells the hǔjiāo,
whose form is that of a fish's body with a snake's tail,
and a head resembling that of a yuānyāng.
Those who eat it will not suffer from swellings,
and it can cure hemorrhoids.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Dānxué,
on which there is much metal and jade.
The Dān River flows from it,
and runs southward into the Bó Sea.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a chicken,
adorned with five colors and patterns,
named Fènghuáng.
The pattern on its head signifies virtue,
the pattern on its wings signifies compliance,
the pattern on its back signifies righteousness,
the pattern on its breast signifies benevolence,
and the pattern on its belly signifies trustworthiness.
This bird,
feeds and drinks naturally,
sings and dances of its own accord,
and when it appears, the world is peaceful and tranquil.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Fāshuǎngzhīshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
abundant in water,
and with many white apes.
The Fànshuǐ River originates here,
and flows southward into the Bóhǎi Sea.
Another four hundred li to the east,
one reaches the end of Máo Mountain.
To its south, there is a valley,
called Yùyí,
where many strange birds dwell,
and from which the gentle south wind emerges.
Four hundred li further east,
one reaches the head of Fēi Shān,
where there is an abundance of metal and jade on its summit,
but no water,
and many venomous reptiles at its base.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Yángjiā,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in water.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Guànxiāng Zhī Shān,
on which there are many trees,
but no grass;
there are many strange birds,
but no beasts.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Jī Shān,
on which there is much metal,
and below it much cinnabar and red ochre.
The Black Water emerges from here,
flowing southward into the sea.
In it, there is a fish called the tuán yú,
which looks like a crucian carp but has bristles like a pig,
and its sound is like that of a suckling pig.
When it appears, there will be a great drought throughout the land.
Another four hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Lìngqiūzhī Shān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant fire.
To its south, there is a valley,
named Zhōng Gǔ,
from which the Tiáofēng wind emerges.
There is a bird here,
shaped like an owl,
with a human face, four eyes, and ears,
named Yóng,
whose call sounds its own name,
and whose appearance signals a great drought throughout the land.
Further east three hundred seventy li,
there is Mount Lúnzhě,
on its summit much metal and jade,
at its base much green mineral pigment.
There is a tree there,
its form like the paper mulberry but with red grain,
its sap like lacquer,
its taste like malt sugar,
those who eat it do not hunger,
it can relieve fatigue,
its name is báigāo,
it can be used to dye jade with blood.
Another five hundred eighty li to the east,
is called Yǔgǎo Mountain,
with many strange beasts,
and many large snakes.
Five hundred eighty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Nányú Zhī Shān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and below it, much water.
There is a cave there,
into which water enters in spring,
emerges in summer,
and closes in winter.
The Zuǒ Shuǐ originates from it,
flowing southeast into the sea,
and there are fènghuáng and yuānchú.
All of the mountains in the third scroll of the Southern Mountains,
from Tiānyú Zhī Shān to Nányú Zhī Shān,
amount to fourteen mountains in total,
spanning six thousand five hundred and thirty li.
Their deities all have dragon bodies and human faces.
For their sacrifices,
a white dog is offered in prayer,
using polished glutinous rice as the sacrificial grain.
To the right are the mountains of the southern classic,
comprising forty mountains in total,
spanning sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty li.
The first mountain of the Huà Shān range in the "Western Mountains Classic",
is called Qiánlái Zhī Shān.
On its summit, there are many pine trees,
and at its base, numerous washing stones.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a sheep but with a horse's tail,
named Qiányáng,
and its fat can be used to cure chapped skin.
Forty-five li to the west,
there is Mount Sōngguǒ.
From it flows the Guàn River,
which runs northward into the Wèi River,
and in it, there is much copper.
There is a bird here,
named Tóngqú,
whose appearance is like a pheasant,
with a black body and red feet,
and it can be used to cure boils.
Another sixty li to the west,
there is Mount Tàihuà,
steep and square-shaped,
its height is five thousand ren,
its breadth is ten li,
where no birds or beasts dwell.
There is a serpent there,
named Féiyì,
with six feet and four wings,
whose appearance causes great drought throughout the land.
Another eighty li to the west,
there is Mount Xiǎohuà.
Its trees are mostly brambles and wolfberries, and its beasts are mostly zuò cattle.
On its northern side, there are many qìng stones,
while on its southern side, there is much tūfú jade.
The birds are mostly red pheasants,
which can ward off fire.
Among its grasses is the bìlì plant,
which looks like crow's moss,
grows on rocks,
and also climbs trees to grow.
Eating it can cure heart pain.
Another eighty li to the west,
there is Mount Fúyú,
on its southern side there is much copper,
on its northern side much iron.
Upon it grows a tree,
named Wénjīng,
its fruit resembles dates,
and it can be used to cure deafness.
Its plants are abundant with Tiáo,
which look like mallows,
bearing red flowers and yellow fruits,
resembling an infant's tongue.
Eating them prevents people from being deluded.
The Fúyú River originates here,
and flows north into the Wèi River.
Its beasts are mostly Cōnglóng,
which resemble sheep but have red manes.
Its birds are mostly Mín,
which resemble kingfishers but have red beaks,
and can be used to ward off fire.
Another sixty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Shícuì.
Its trees are mostly zōng and nán,
and its grass is mostly tiáo,
which looks like chives,
with white flowers and black fruit.
Eating it can cure scabies.
On its sunny side, there is much túfú jade,
and on its shady side, much copper.
The Guàn River flows out from here,
running northward into the Yú River.
In it, there is flowing red ochre,
which, when applied to cattle and horses, prevents illness.
Another seventy li to the west,
there is Yīngshān,
on which there are many niǔ and jiāng trees,
on its northern side there is much iron,
and on its southern side there is much red gold.
Yù Shuǐ flows from here,
running northward into Zhāo Shuǐ,
in which there are many bàng fish,
which look like turtles,
and make a sound like sheep.
On its sunny side, there are many arrow bamboos,
and among the beasts, there are many zuò niú and qián yáng.
There is a bird here,
whose shape resembles a quail,
with a yellow body and a red beak,
named féi yí.
Eating it can cure epidemic diseases,
and it can kill insects.
Another fifty-two li to the west,
there is a mountain called Zhú Shān,
on which there are many tall trees,
and on its northern side, much iron.
There is a plant here,
named Huáng Guàn,
whose shape is like the tree of heaven,
with leaves like hemp,
white flowers and red fruit,
whose appearance is like red ochre.
Bathing with it cures scabies,
and it can also be used to treat swelling.
The Bamboo River originates here,
flowing northward into the Wei River.
On its southern slopes grow many arrow bamboos,
and abundant gray jade.
The Dan River emerges from this place,
running southeast to join the Luo River.
In its waters are numerous crystals,
and many human-faced fish.
There is a beast dwelling here,
shaped like a pig with white fur,
its hairs as large as hairpins with black tips,
which it shoots at objects.
It is named the Háo Zhì.
Another one hundred twenty li to the west is called Fú Shān,
with abundant Pàn mù,
having leaves like trifoliate orange but without thorns,
where tree-dwelling insects inhabit.
There is a plant,
named Xūn cǎo,
with leaves like hemp and a square stem,
bearing red flowers and black fruits,
its fragrance resembling that of méi wú,
and wearing it can cure skin diseases.
Another seventy li to the west,
there is Yúcì Mountain,
from which the Qī River flows,
running northward into the Wèi River.
On its heights grow many oak and evergreen oak trees,
while below, there are abundant arrow bamboos.
On its northern slopes, there is much red copper,
and on its southern slopes, plenty of Yīngyuán jade.
There is a beast here,
which looks like a long-armed monkey,
adept at throwing,
and its name is Xiāo.
There is a bird here,
which resembles an owl,
with a human face and one foot,
named Tuófēi,
it appears in winter and hibernates in summer,
and wearing its feathers makes one fearless of thunder.
Another one hundred fifty miles to the west,
there is Shí Shān,
which has no grass or trees.
The Zhú Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing northward into the Wèi,
and within it, there is much crystal.
Another hundred seventy li to the west,
there is a mountain called Nánshān,
on which grows much red millet-like sand.
The Dānshuǐ River originates here,
flowing northward into the Wèi River.
Among the beasts, fierce leopards are plentiful,
and among the birds, cuckoos abound.
Another hundred eighty li to the west,
stands Dàshí Mountain,
its summit rich with paper mulberry and oak trees,
its base abundant in wild jujube and evergreen oak,
its northern slopes yielding silver,
and its southern slopes yielding white jade.
The Cén River flows from here,
running northward into the Wèi River,
while the Qīng River also originates here,
flowing southward into the Hàn River.
Another three hundred twenty li to the west,
there is Mount Bōzhǒng.
The Hànshuǐ River flows out from here,
and runs southeast into the Miǎn River;
the Xiāoshuǐ River also flows out from here,
running north into the Tāngshuǐ River.
On its summit, there are many peach-branch bamboos and hook-end bamboos.
Among the beasts, there are many rhinoceroses, wild buffaloes, bears, and brown bears;
among the birds, there are many white pheasants and red pheasants.
There is a plant here,
whose leaves are like the huì orchid,
and whose root is like the jiégěng root,
with black flowers but bearing no fruit.
It is called gǔróng,
and eating it causes one to be childless.
Three hundred and fifty li further west,
there is a mountain called Tiāndìzhīshān,
on its summit grow abundant palm trees and nanmu,
while at its base flourish reeds and orchids.
There is a beast dwelling there,
whose form resembles that of a dog,
named Xībiān,
and anyone who uses its skin as a mat will be free from bewitchment.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling a quail,
with black patterns and red neck feathers,
named Lì,
eating it cures hemorrhoids.
There is a plant here,
its form resembling a sunflower,
its scent like that of míwú,
named Dùhéng,
it can make horses run swiftly,
eating it cures goiters.
Three hundred eighty li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Gāotúzhīshān.
A river flows out from it,
running westward into the Zhūzīzhīshuǐ.
The Túshuǐ also originates here,
flowing southward into the Jíhuòzhīshuǐ.
On its southern slopes, there is an abundance of cinnabar grains,
while its northern slopes are rich in silver and gold,
and its heights are covered with cinnamon trees.
There is a white stone found there,
named Yù,
which can be used to poison rats.
There is a plant,
shaped like dried ginger,
with leaves resembling mallow but red on the back,
named Wútiáo,
which can be used to poison rats.
There is a beast,
shaped like a deer with a white tail,
having horse hooves, human hands, and four horns,
named Juérú.
There is a bird,
shaped like an owl with human feet,
named Shùsī,
eating it cures goiters.
Another one hundred eighty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Huángshān,
devoid of grasses and trees,
but abundant with arrow bamboos.
The Pàn Shuǐ originates from here,
flows westward into the Chì Shuǐ,
and contains much jade.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox,
with dark blue-black color and large eyes,
named Mào.
There is a bird here,
shaped like an owl,
with blue feathers and a red beak,
a human-like tongue capable of speech,
named Yīngmóu.
Two hundred li further west,
there is Cuì Shān,
on its summit there are many palm trees and nanmu trees,
at its foot many arrow bamboos,
on its sunny side much gold and jade,
on its shady side many yaks, ling antelopes, and musk deer;
among its birds there are many Xiè,
their form like magpies,
red and black with two heads and four feet,
they can be used to ward off fire.
Another two hundred fifty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Guī Shān,
which stands by the Western Sea.
It has no grass or trees,
but abundant jade.
The Qī River flows out from here,
running westward into the sea.
In it, there are many colorful stones and gold,
as well as abundant cinnabar granules.
Overall, the first section of the "Western Classic,"
stretches from Mount Qiánlái to Mount Guī,
covering a total of nineteen mountains,
spanning two thousand nine hundred and fifty-seven li.
Mount Huà is the ancestral tomb,
and the sacrificial rites for it
involve the grand offering of livestock.
Mount Yú is a deity,
For the sacrifices, candles are used,
a hundred-day fast is observed with a hundred sacrificial animals,
offerings are buried with a hundred pieces of jade,
the wine amounts to a hundred vessels,
and adorned with a hundred jade tablets and a hundred bi discs.
As for the remaining seventeen mountains of this kind,
all are sacrificed to using one whole sheep.
The candles are made from unburned hundred herbs,
and the white mats are adorned with colored patterns of uniform purity.
The first mountain of the Second Western Classic,
is called Qián Shān,
on its summit there is much copper,
at its foot there is much jade,
and its trees are mostly nǐu and jiāng.
Two hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Tàimào.
Its southern side is rich in gold,
while its northern side abounds in iron.
The Luò River originates here,
flowing eastward into the Hé River,
and in it are many patterned jades
and numerous white snakes.
Another one hundred seventy li to the west,
there is Mount Shùlì,
on which there is much yellow gold,
and below it much silver.
Among its trees are many niǔ and jiāng trees,
and among its birds, many parrots.
The Chǔ River flows out from here
and runs southward to empty into the Wèi River,
in which there are many pearls.
Another one hundred fifty li to the west is called Gāo Shān,
on its summit there is much silver,
at its base much green jasper and realgar,
among its trees many are palms,
among its grasses many are bamboos.
Jīng Shuǐ emerges from here,
and flows eastward into Wèi,
within it are many musical stones and green jasper.
Three hundred li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Nǚchuáng.
On its sunny side, there is much red copper,
and on its shady side, much shíniè (a type of mineral).
Among the beasts, there are many tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and wild buffaloes.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a pheasant with five-colored patterns,
named the luánniǎo.
When it appears, all under heaven is peaceful and tranquil.
Two hundred li further to the west,
there is a mountain called Lóngshǒu.
On its southern side, there is abundant gold,
and on its northern side, much iron.
The Tiáo River flows from here,
running southeast into the Jīng River,
where there is an abundance of beautiful jade.
Another two hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Lùtái Zhī Shān.
On its summit, there is an abundance of white jade,
and at its base, much silver.
Among the beasts, there are many zuò niú, qián yáng, and bái háo.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a rooster but with a human face,
named fú xī.
Its call sounds like its own name,
and when it appears, there will be warfare.
Two hundred li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Niǎowēi.
On its southern side, there are many resonant stones,
on its northern side, much sandalwood and paper mulberry,
and within it, many Nǚchuáng plants.
The Niǎowēi River flows out from here,
running westward into the Chìshuǐ River,
and in it, there is much cinnabar sand.
Another four hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Xiǎocìzhī Shān,
on which there is much white jade,
and beneath it much red copper.
There is a beast dwelling there,
whose form is like that of an ape,
with a white head and red feet,
named Zhūyàn.
When it appears, great warfare will arise.
Three hundred li further west,
there is a mountain called Dàcìzhī Shān.
On its southern side, there is much white clay,
and on its northern side, much green jade.
Among its animals are many zuò niú and líng yáng.
Another four hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Xūnwú,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metals and jade.
Another four hundred li to the west,
lies the mountain called Dǐyáng Zhī Shān,
where the trees are mostly jì, nán, and yùzhāng,
and the beasts are mostly rhinoceroses, sì, tigers, zhuó, and zuò oxen.
Another two hundred fifty li to the west,
there is Mount Zhòngshòu,
on which there is much Tūfú jade,
and below it there are many sandalwood and paper mulberry trees,
as well as abundant gold.
Among the beasts, there are many rhinoceroses and wild buffaloes.
Another five hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Huángrén.
On its summit, there is much metal and jade,
and at its base, abundant green and red orpiment.
The Huáng River originates here,
flows westward, and empties into the Chì River,
in which there is much cinnabar sand.
Another three hundred li to the west,
there is Mount Zhōnghuáng,
on which there is much yellow gold,
and below which there is much orchid and pear.
Another three hundred fifty li to the west,
there is Mount Xīhuáng,
on its sunny side there is much gold,
on its shady side much iron,
and among its beasts are many elk, deer, and zuò niú.
Another three hundred fifty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Láishān,
where the trees are mostly sandalwood and paper mulberry,
and the birds are mostly Luóluó birds,
which eat humans.
Overall, the beginning of the "Second Western Mountains" classic,
from Qián Shān to Lái Shān,
comprises a total of seventeen mountains,
spanning four thousand one hundred and forty li.
Among them, ten deities
all have human faces and horse bodies.
Seven of these deities have human faces and ox bodies,
with four legs and one arm,
walking while holding a staff,
and are known as the gods of flying beasts;
When sacrificing to them,
the fur offerings use a young pig and sheep,
with white sedge mats as the seating.
As for the ten ranks of deities,
when sacrificing to them,
the fur offering is one rooster,
tied but without rice offerings;
the fur is colored.
The first mountain of the Western Third Range,
is called Chóngwúzhīshān,
located south of the river,
looking north to Zhǒngsuì,
south to Yáozhīzé,
west to Dìzhībó and Shòuzhīqiū,
and east to Yānyuān.
There is a tree here,
with round leaves and white calyxes,
bearing red flowers with black veins,
its fruit resembles that of the trifoliate orange,
and eating it benefits one's descendants.
There is a beast here,
which looks like a long-tailed monkey with patterned arms,
has the stripes of a tiger and is skilled at throwing,
named Jǔfù.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling a wild duck,
but with one wing and one eye,
it must pair up to fly,
named Mánmán,
when it appears, there will be great floods throughout the land.
Three hundred li to the northwest,
there is a mountain called Chángshā.
The Cǐ River flows from here,
runs northward, and empties into the Yōu River.
There are no grasses or trees,
but an abundance of azurite and realgar.
Another three hundred seventy li to the northwest,
there is Mount Bùzhōu.
To the north, one gazes upon the mountains of Zhūpí,
overlooking those lofty peaks of Yuèchóng.
To the east, one looks upon the Yōu Swamp,
where the Yellow River submerges underground,
its source bubbling and gushing turbulently.
Here grows a fine fruit,
its fruit resembling a peach,
its leaves like those of a jujube tree,
with yellow blossoms and red calyxes.
Eating it relieves fatigue.
Another four hundred twenty li to the northwest,
there is a mountain called Mìshān.
On its summit grows much Dān Mù,
with round leaves and red stems,
yellow flowers and red fruits,
whose taste is like sweet syrup,
and eating them prevents hunger.
The Dān Shuǐ flows out from here,
running westward into Jì Zé,
wherein there is much white jade.
There is jade ointment,
its source bubbling and boiling,
which the Huángdì ate and enjoyed.
From it, dark jade was born.
Where the jade ointment emerges,
it is used to irrigate the cinnabar tree.
The cinnabar tree grows for five years,
then its five colors become clear,
and its five flavors become fragrant.
The Yellow Emperor then took the jade blossoms from Mìshān Mountain,
and cast them upon the sunny side of Zhōngshān Mountain.
The jade of jǐnyú proved to be of the finest quality,
firm, plump, fine, and dense,
turbidly black yet radiant.
Five colors emanated and arose,
thereby harmonizing the soft and the hard.
Heaven, Earth, and the spirits,
Are fed and honored with offerings;
The nobleman wears them,
To ward off inauspiciousness.
From Mì Shān to Zhōng Shān,
A distance of four hundred and sixty miles,
The entire area is marshland.
Here abound strange birds, monstrous beasts, and peculiar fish,
All of which are extraordinary creatures.
Another four hundred twenty li to the northwest,
there is a mountain called Zhōngshān,
whose son is named Gǔ,
with a human face and a dragon's body.
He, together with Qīnpéi, killed Bǎojiāng south of Kūnlún,
and the Emperor then executed them east of Zhōngshān at a place called Yáo'àn.
Qīnpéi transformed into a great eagle,
resembling a hawk with black markings,
a white head, a red beak, and tiger claws,
its cry like that of the morning crane.
Its appearance signals the coming of great armies;
the drum also transforms into a Jùnniǎo,
which looks like an owl,
with red feet and a straight beak,
yellow patterns and a white head,
its call resembling that of a swan,
and wherever it appears, that region will suffer a severe drought.
Another one hundred eighty li to the west,
there is Mount Tàiqì.
The Guàn River flows out from here,
running westward into the Flowing Sands.
Here there are many Wényáo fish,
shaped like carp,
with fish bodies and bird wings,
blue patterns and white heads,
and red beaks.
It often travels the Western Sea,
roams the Eastern Sea,
flying by night.
Its call resembles that of the luánjī,
its flavor is sour and sweet,
eating it cures madness,
and its appearance heralds a year of great abundance across the land.
Further west three hundred twenty li,
there is Mount Huáijiāng.
The Qiūshí River flows out from here,
and runs northward into the Yōu River.
In it are many mother-of-pearl snails,
on it much green orpiment,
and abundant stores of lánggān jade, jade, gold,
its sunny side abounds in cinnabar granules,
its shady side is rich in colorful gold and silver.
This is indeed the Emperor's Level Garden,
deity Yīngzhāo governs it,
his form has a horse's body and a human face,
tiger stripes and bird wings,
he patrols the four seas,
his voice is like the pomegranate.
Looking south toward Kūnlún,
its light blazes fiercely,
its aura swirls intensely.
Looking west, there lies the great marsh,
where Hòu Jì once delved;
within it, there is much jade,
and on its shady side, there are many Yáo trees bearing Ruò fruit.
Looking north, one sees the Zhū Pí mountains,
where Huái Guǐ Lí Lún resides,
and where eagles and sparrowhawks make their home.
Looking east at the fourfold Huán Shān,
where destitute ghosts dwell,
each occupying a section.
There lies an overflowing river,
its waters clear and rippling.
A celestial deity resides there,
whose form resembles an ox,
yet with eight legs, two heads, and a horse's tail,
its cry like that of a pheasant,
and when it appears, warfare erupts in its domain.
Four hundred li to the southwest,
there is a mound called Kūnlún,
which serves as the earthly capital of the Heavenly Emperor,
guarded by the deity Lù Wú.
This deity has the body of a tiger with nine tails,
a human face, and tiger claws;
this god
is in charge of the nine divisions of heaven and the imperial gardens' seasons.
There is a beast there,
shaped like a goat but
with four horns,
named Tǔ Lóu,
which eats humans.
There is a bird here,
which looks like a bee,
as large as a mandarin duck,
named Qīnyuán,
whose sting kills birds and beasts,
and withers trees when it stings them.
There is another bird, named Chúnniǎo,
which is in charge of all the garments of the Emperor.
There is a tree,
shaped like a pear-leaved crabapple,
with yellow blossoms and red fruit,
tasting like a plum but without a pit,
named shātáng,
which can ward off water,
and eating it prevents people from drowning.
There is a grass,
named píncǎo,
shaped like a sunflower and tasting like an onion,
eating it relieves fatigue.
The Hé River originates here,
flowing south and then east into Wúdá.
The Chì River originates here,
flowing southeast into the waters of Fàntiān.
The Yáng River originates here,
flowing southwest into the waters of Chǒutú.
The Hēi River originates here,
flowing west into Dàyú.
Here dwell many strange birds and beasts.
Another three hundred seventy li to the west,
there is Mount Lèyóu.
The Táo River flows out from here,
running westward into Jì Marsh,
where there is an abundance of white jade.
In it, there are many Huà fish,
which look like snakes but have four legs,
and they eat fish.
Traveling four hundred li westward by water,
one reaches the Flowing Sands,
and another two hundred li brings one to Mount Luómǔ.
The deity Chángchéng presides over it,
embodying the nine virtues of heaven.
This deity has a form resembling a human but with a leopard's tail.
On its summit, there is an abundance of jade,
while at its base, there are many blue stones but no water.
Three hundred and fifty li further west,
there is a mountain called Yù Shān,
where Xī Wáng Mǔ resides.
Xī Wáng Mǔ has a form resembling a human,
with a leopard's tail, tiger's teeth, and is skilled at howling,
with disheveled hair and wearing a headdress,
and she is in charge of the calamities of heaven and the five destructive forces.
There is a beast here,
whose form is like a dog but with leopard-like patterns,
its horns are like those of an ox,
its name is Jiǎo,
its sound is like a barking dog,
and when it appears, the state will have a great harvest.
There is a bird here,
whose form is like a pheasant and is red,
named Shèngyù,
it eats fish,
its sound is like a record,
and when it appears, the state will have a great flood.
Another four hundred eighty li to the west,
there is a place called Xuānyuán Hill,
where no grass or trees grow.
The Xún River flows out from here,
running southward into the Black Water,
and in it are many cinnabar granules,
as well as abundant blue orpiment.
Another three hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Jīshí,
at the foot of which lies a stone gate,
through which the Yellow River surges and flows southwest.
This mountain
contains every kind of thing in existence.
Another two hundred li to the west,
there is Mount Chángliú,
where the god White Emperor Shàohào resides.
All the beasts there have patterned tails,
and all the birds have patterned heads.
There is an abundance of patterned jade stones.
It is indeed the palace of the Round God Kuǐshì.
This deity
is in charge of overseeing the reflections of sunlight.
Two hundred and eighty li further west,
there is a mountain called Zhāng'é,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in jasper and jade.
Strange phenomena occur there.
There is a beast,
shaped like a red leopard,
with five tails and one horn,
whose sound is like striking stones,
and its name is Zhēng.
There is a bird here,
its form like a crane,
with one foot,
red patterns on a blue body and a white beak,
named Bìfāng,
its call is its own name,
and when it appears, there will be freak fires in its district.
Another three hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Yīnshān.
The Zhuóyù River originates from it,
and flows south into Fānzé.
In the river, there are many patterned shells.
There is a beast here,
which looks like a wildcat with a white head,
named Tiāngǒu.
Its cry sounds like "liú liú,"
and it can be used to ward off evil.
Two hundred li further west,
there is a mountain called Fúdàng,
with many palm trees and nanmu trees on its summit,
and abundant metal and jade at its base.
The deity Jiāng Yí dwells there.
This mountain
often experiences strange rains,
and is a place where winds and clouds arise.
Two hundred twenty li further to the west,
there is Mount Sānwēi,
where the three green birds dwell.
This mountain spans an area of a hundred li.
Upon it, there is a beast,
shaped like an ox,
with a white body and four horns,
its fur resembling a draped straw raincoat,
named Àoyē,
which eats humans.
There is also a bird there,
with one head and three bodies,
shaped like a lark,
named Chī.
Another one hundred ninety miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Guīshān,
abundant with jade but devoid of ordinary stones.
The deity Qítóng resides there,
whose voice is always like the sound of bells and chimes.
At its foot, there are numerous accumulated snakes.
Another three hundred fifty miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Tiānshān,
rich in gold and jade,
and with blue and red orpiment.
Yīngshuǐ originates from here,
and flows southwest into Tānggǔ.
There is a deity here,
whose form resembles a yellow sack,
red as cinnabar fire,
with six feet and four wings,
chaotic and without face or eyes,
yet it knows singing and dancing,
and is truly Dìjiāng.
Two hundred and ninety li further west,
there is Mount Yōu,
where the deity Rùshōu resides.
On its summit, there is an abundance of Yīngduǎn jade,
on its sunny side, much Jīnyú jade,
and on its shady side, a great deal of green realgar.
This mountain
looks westward to where the sun sets,
its aura is rounded,
and it is under the charge of the deity Hóngguāng.
Traveling a hundred li westward by water,
one arrives at Yìwàng Mountain.
It has no grass or trees,
but abounds in metal and jade.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a wildcat,
with one eye and three tails,
named Huān.
Its cry is like a hundred sounds being snatched away,
and it can ward off evil omens.
Consuming it cures jaundice.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling a crow,
with three heads, six tails, and adept at laughing,
named Qíyú.
Consuming it prevents people from having nightmares,
and it can also ward off evil.
In general, the beginning of the "Western Third Classic,"

spanning six thousand seven hundred and forty-four li.

The ritual for sacrificing to them
involves burying one auspicious jade,
using millet as the sacrificial grain.
The first mountain of the "Xī Cì Sì Jīng" is called Yīn Shān,

Yīn Shuǐ emanates from here,
flowing west to pour into Luò.
Fifty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Láo Shān,
abundant with zǐ grass.
The Ruò Shuǐ originates here,
and flows westward into the Luò River.
Fifty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Pígǔ Zhī Shān. The Ěr Shuǐ originates from it,

where there is an abundance of zǐ and jasper.
One hundred and seventy li to the north,
there is a mountain called Shēn Shān,
with many paper mulberry and oak trees on its summit,
and numerous wild jujube and oak trees at its base.
On its southern side, there is an abundance of metal and jade.
The Qū Shuǐ River originates from here,
and flows eastward into the Hé River.
Two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Niǎoshān.
On its summit, there are many mulberry trees,
and at its base, numerous paper mulberry trees.
On its northern side, there is abundant iron,
while on its southern side, much jade.
The Rǔshuǐ River originates here
and flows eastward into the Hé River.
Another one hundred and twenty li to the north,
there is Shàngshēn Zhī Shān,
on its summit there are no grasses or trees,
but there are many large rocks,
below there are many hazels and thorny bushes,
and among the beasts, many are white deer.
Among the birds, many are dānghù,
their form resembling pheasants,
they fly using their beards,
and eating them prevents eye blinking.
Tāng Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing eastward into the Hé.
Another hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Zhūcì,
from which the Zhūcì River originates,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Yellow River.
This mountain
has abundant trees but no grass,
and neither birds nor beasts dwell there,
yet it is teeming with numerous snakes.
Another hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Hào Shān,
where the trees are mostly lacquer and palm,
and the grasses are largely yào, xiāo, and qiōngqióng. There is an abundance of lěng stones.
Duān Shuǐ originates from here,
and flows eastward into the Hé River.
Another two hundred twenty li to the north,
there is Mount Yú,
on its northern side there is much iron,
on its southern side there is much copper,
among its beasts are many white wolves and white tigers,
among its birds are many white pheasants and white long-tailed pheasants.
The Shēng River emerges from here,
and flows eastward into the Hé River.
Two hundred fifty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Báiyú Zhī Shān.
Its upper slopes abound with pine and cypress trees,
while its lower parts are rich in oak and sandalwood.
Among the beasts, many are zuò niú and qián yáng,
and among the birds, many are owls.
The Luò Shuǐ emerges from its southern side,
flowing eastward into the Wèi River;
the Jiā Shuǐ emerges from its northern side,
flowing eastward into the Shēng Shuǐ.
Three hundred li to the northwest,
there is a mountain called Yóushǒu,
with no grass or trees,
and snow in both winter and summer.
The Shēn River originates from its summit,
and flows hidden beneath it,
where there is an abundance of white jade.
Another fifty-five li to the west,
is the Jīnggǔ Mountain,
from which the Jīng River originates,
flowing southeast into the Wèi River,
and here there is an abundance of white metal and white jade.
Another one hundred twenty li to the west,
there is Gāng Shān,
abundant with lacquer trees and much
Túfú jade.
Gāng Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing north into the Wèi River.
Here dwell many Shénkuí,
whose forms have human faces and beast bodies,
with one foot and one hand,
and whose sounds are like chanting.
Two hundred li further west,
one reaches the end of Gāng Mountain.
The Luò River emerges from here,
flowing northward and emptying into the Yellow River.
In it dwell many mánmán creatures,
which have the body of a rat and the head of a turtle,
and their cry is like that of a barking dog.
Another three hundred fifty li to the west,
stands Yīngdī Mountain,
its summit abundant with lacquer trees,
its foothills rich in metal and jade,
its birds and beasts all white.
Yuān River flows forth from here,
running northward into Língyáng Marsh.
Here dwell many Rǎnyí fish,
with fish-like bodies and snake-like heads,
six feet,
and eyes resembling horse ears.
Eating them prevents people from having nightmares,
and can ward off evil.
Another three hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Zhōngqǔ.
On its southern side, there is much jade,
while on its northern side, there is much realgar, white jade, and gold.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a horse with a white body and black tail,
having one horn,
tiger-like teeth and claws,
and a sound like that of a drum.
Its name is Bó,
it preys on tigers and leopards,
and it can ward off weapons.
There is a tree,
which looks like a pear tree,
with round leaves and red fruits,
the fruits as large as a quince,
named Guāimù,
and eating it increases one's strength.
Two hundred sixty li further west,
there is a mountain called Guī Shān.
On its summit there is a beast,
shaped like an ox,
with hedgehog-like bristles,
named Qióngqí,
whose cry resembles that of a howling dog,
and it devours humans. The Méng Shuǐ originates here,
flowing south into the Yáng Shuǐ,
in which there are many yellow shells
and Luó Yú,
fish with bird-like wings,
whose sound is like that of mandarin ducks,
and whose appearance foretells great floods in the city.
Two hundred twenty li further west,
there is a mountain called Niǎoshǔtóngxué Zhī Shān,
on which there are many white tigers and white jade.
The Wèi Shuǐ originates here,
and flows eastward into the Hé.
In it, there are many shāo fish,
which resemble sturgeon in appearance.
If they leap and stir, then the city will face great military conflict.
The river originates from its west,
flowing westward into the Hànshuǐ.
There are many tuóbǐ fish,
which look like overturned pots,
with bird heads and fish fins and tails,
their calls resembling the sound of chime stones,
and they give birth to pearls and jade.
Three hundred and sixty li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Yānzī,
on which there is much red wood.
Its leaves are like those of the paper mulberry, and its
fruit is as large as a melon,
with red skin and black patterns.
Eating it cures jaundice,
and it can be used to ward off fire.
On its southern side, there are many turtles,
and on its northern side, there is much jade.
The Sháo River flows out from there,
running westward into the sea,
in which there are many whetstones.
There is a beast here,
whose form is like a horse's body with bird's wings,
a human face and a snake's tail,
fond of lifting people,
named Shúhú.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles an owl with a human face,
a monkey's body and a dog's tail,
its call sounds like its own name,
and when it appears, the region will suffer a great drought.

there are a total of nineteen mountains,
spanning three thousand six hundred and eighty li.
For the sacrificial rites to their deities,
a white chicken is always used in prayers.

with white sedge grass serving as the mat.
The mountains of the Western Classic,
in total seventy-seven mountains,
spanning seventeen thousand five hundred and seventeen li.
The first mountain in the Classic of the Northern Mountains
is called the Dānhú Mountains,
where many machine trees grow,
and on its summit, there are abundant flowering grasses.
The Féng River originates here,
flowing westward into the Yōu River,
and in it, there are many purple stones and patterned stones.
Another two hundred and fifty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Qiúrúzhīshān.
On its summit, there is much copper,
and at its base, much jade,
but no grasses or trees.
The Huá Shuǐ originates from here,
and flows westward into the waters of Zhūpí.
In it there are many slippery fish,
which look like eels,
with red backs,
and their call sounds like the wú tree.
Eating them can cure warts.
In it there are many water horses,
which look like horses,
with patterned forelegs and ox tails,
and their call sounds like a human shout.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dài Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and below it much green jasper.
There is a beast here,
whose shape is like a horse,
with a single horn that is rough,
and its name is Huān Shū,
which can be used to ward off fire.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling a crow,
with five colors and crimson patterns,
named Qíyú,
it naturally possesses both male and female characteristics,
and eating it prevents boils.
The Péng River originates here,
flowing westward into the waters of Pí Lake,
where there are many Shū fish,
their shape like a chicken
with red feathers,
three tails, six feet, and four eyes,
their call resembling that of a magpie,
and consuming them can alleviate sorrow.
Another four hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Qiáomíng Zhī Shān,
from which the Qiáo River flows,
running westward into the Yellow River.
In it, there are many Héluó fish,
with one head and ten bodies,
whose sound is like a barking dog,
and eating them can cure abscesses.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a badger with red bristles,
its call sounds like "liú liú",
named Mèng Huái,
which can be used to ward off evil.
This mountain,
has no grass or trees,
but abounds in realgar and orpiment.
Another three hundred and fifty li to the north,
there is Mount Zhuōguāng.
The Xiāo River flows out from here,
and runs westward into the Yellow River.
In it, there are many Xíxí fish,
which look like magpies but have ten wings,
with scales all at the tips of their feathers.
Their sound is like that of a magpie,
and they can be used to ward off fire.
Eating them prevents jaundice.
On its heights, there are many pines and cypresses,
while at its base, there are abundant palm and oak trees.
Among its beasts, there are many lingyang antelopes,
and among its birds, there are many fan birds.
Another three hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Guó Shān,
on which there is much lacquer,
and at its foot much phoenix tree and wingceltis,
on its sunny side much jade,
and on its shady side much iron.
The Yī Shuǐ emerges from here,
and flows west into the Hé.
Among its beasts are many camels,
and among its birds many寓言 (yù),
which have the form of rats but bird wings,
their cry is like that of a goat,
and they can be used to ward off weapons.
Another four hundred li to the north,
one reaches the tail of Guó Mountain,
where there is much jade but no stone.
Yú Water flows out from there,
running westward into the Hé River,
and in it are many patterned shells.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dānxūn,
on which there are many ailanthus and cypress trees,
and among the grasses, plenty of chives and scallions,
as well as abundant cinnabar and red ochre.
The Xūn River flows from here,
running westward into the Táng River.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a rat,
with a rabbit's head and a deer's ears,
its cry like that of a barking dog,
which flies by means of its tail,
named the ěrshǔ.
Eating it prevents bloating,
and it can also ward off all poisons.
Further north two hundred eighty li,
is called Shízhězhī Shān,
on it there are no grasses or trees,
but much yáo jasper.
Cǐ Shuǐ emerges from here,
and flows west into the Hé,
there is a beast here,
its form like a leopard,
with a patterned forehead and white body,
named Mèngjí,
it is good at hiding,
its call sounds like its name.
Another one hundred and ten li to the north,
there is a mountain called Biānchūnzhīshān, abundant with
scallions, peaches, mallows, leeks, and plums.
The Gàngshuǐ River originates here,
and flows westward into the Yōuzé Marsh.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a macaque with a patterned body,
skilled at laughing,
and when it sees people, it lies down,
named Yōuyàn,
whose call is its own name.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Mànlián Zhī Shān,
on which there are no grasses or trees.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a macaque but has a mane,
a cow's tail, patterned forelimbs, and horse's hooves.
When it sees a person, it laughs,
and its name is Zúzī.
Its call is the sound of its own name.
There is a bird,
that lives in flocks and flies in groups,
its feathers resemble those of a female pheasant,
named Jiāo,
its call echoes its own name,
eating it cures rheumatism.
Another one hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Shànzhāngzhīshān,
on which there are no grasses or trees.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a leopard but with a long tail,
a human head and ox ears,
one eye,
named Zhūjiān,
skilled at roaring,
when walking it holds its tail in its mouth,
when resting it coils its tail.
There is a bird here,
which looks like a pheasant,
with a patterned head, white wings, and yellow feet,
named Bái Yè,
eating it can cure sore throats,
and it can also heal convulsions.
The Lì River originates here,
and flows southward into the Gāng River.
Another three hundred twenty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Guàntízhīshān,
on which there are many ailanthus and mulberry trees,
and at its foot, much quicksand,
as well as numerous whetstones.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a cow but with a white tail,
and its cry sounds like a call; its name
is Nàfù.
There is a bird here,
which looks like a female pheasant with a human face,
leaps upon seeing people,
named Sǒngsī,
its call sounds like its own name.
The Jiànghán River originates from here,
flows westward into the Yōu Swamp,
and contains much magnetite within it.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Pānhóu,
on its summit abundant with pines and cypresses,
at its foot plentiful with hazels and thorny bushes,
on its sunny side rich in jade,
and on its shady side abundant in iron.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox,
with hair growing on its four joints,
named the yak.
The Biān River flows out from here,
and runs southward into the Swamp of Lì.
Another two hundred thirty li to the north,
is the mountain called Xiǎoxián Zhī Shān,
where no grasses or trees grow,
and there is snow in both winter and summer.
Two hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dàxián Zhī Shān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant jade at its base.
This mountain is square in shape,
and cannot be climbed.
There is a serpent named Cháng Shé,
whose fur is like the bristles of a pig,
and whose sound resembles that of a watchman's clapper.
Further north three hundred twenty li,
there is a mountain called Dūn Hōng,
on its summit grows an abundance of palm and nanmu trees,
and at its base, plenty of purple grass.
The River Dūn Hōng originates here,
flowing westward into the Yōu Swamp.
It emerges from the northeast corner of Kūnlún,
truly serving as the source of the Yellow River.
In its waters are many red salmon,
among its beasts, numerous rhinoceroses and yaks,
and among its birds, many cuckoos.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Shǎoxiánzhīshān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in green jasper.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox,
but with a red body, a human face, and horse hooves,
named Yàyǔ,
whose cry sounds like a baby,
and it eats people.
The Dūnshuǐ River originates here,
flowing east into the waters of Yànmén,
where there are many Pèipèi fish,
and eating them will kill a person.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Yùfǎzhīshān.
The Huáizézhīshhuǐ River originates from it,
and flows northeast into Tàizé.
In it, there are many Zǎoyú fish,
which look like carp but have chicken feet,
and eating them can cure warts.
There is a beast there,
which resembles a dog but has a human face,
is skilled at throwing,
and laughs upon seeing people,
its name is Shānhún,
it moves like the wind,
and its appearance causes great winds throughout the world.
Another hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Běiyuè,
abundant with trifoliate orange trees, thorny bushes, and hardwoods.
A beast dwells there,
its form resembling an ox
with four horns, human eyes, and pig ears,
named Zhūhuái.
Its cry is like the call of a wild goose,
and it devours humans.
The Zhūhuái River originates here,
flowing westward into the Xiāo River,
where many Qí fish are found.
These fish have the body of a fish and the head of a dog,
their sound like that of an infant,
and eating them cures madness.
Another hundred eighty li to the north,
there is Mount Húnxī,
which has no grass or trees,
but abundant copper and jade.
The Xiāo River flows out from here,
and runs northwest to empty into the sea.
There is a snake with one head and two bodies,
named Féiyí,
whose appearance causes great drought in the state.
Another fifty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Běidān,
with no grasses or trees,
but abundant with scallions and chives.
Another hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Pí Chāi Zhī Shān,
which has no grasses or trees,
but many horses.
Another one hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Běixiǎn,
where many horses are found.
The Xiǎn River flows out from here,
and runs northwest to pour into the Túwú River.
Another hundred and seventy li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dī Shān,
with many horses.
There is a beast here,
whose appearance is like a leopard but with a patterned head,
named yǎo. The
Dī River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into Tài Zé,
where there are many dragon-turtles.
All the mountains recorded in the Classic of the Mountains of the North,
from Dānhú Mountain to Dī Mountain,
amount to twenty-five mountains in total,
spanning five thousand four hundred and ninety li.
The deities of these mountains all have human faces and snake bodies.
When offering sacrifices to them,
use a rooster and a pig buried with their hair,
and a piece of auspicious jade in the form of a guī tablet,
burying them without offering grain.
The people north of these mountains
all eat their food raw, without cooking it.
The head of the second range of the Northern Mountains,
lies east of the River,
its head resting on the Fén,
is named the Guǎncén Mountains.
On its heights, there are no trees but much grass,
and below it, there is much jade.
The Fén River flows from here,
and runs west to empty into the River.
Another two hundred fifty li to the north,
there is Mount Shǎoyáng,
on which there is much jade,
and at its foot much red silver.
The Suān River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into the Fén River,
in which there is much fine red ochre.
Another fifty li to the north,
there is Mount Xiànyōng,
on which there is much jade,
and below it much copper.
Among the beasts, there are many wild donkeys and elk,
and among the birds, many white pheasants and white quails.
The Jìn River originates here,
flowing southeast into the Fén River.
In it, there are many cáo fish,
which resemble minnows but have red scales,
and make a sound like scolding.
Eating them prevents arrogance.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Húqí,
which has no grasses or trees,
but is rich in green jasper.
The Shèng River originates here,
flowing northeast to join the Fén River,
and in it there is much dark green jade.
Further north three hundred fifty li,
is called Báishā Shān,
its expanse measures three hundred li,
entirely sand,
without grass, trees, birds, or beasts.
Wěi Shuǐ emerges from its top,
and submerges beneath it,
here there is much white jade.
Another four hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Ěrshì,
with no grass or trees,
and no water.
Further north three hundred eighty li,
is called Kuáng Shān,
without grass or trees.
This mountain,
has snow in both winter and summer.
Kuáng Shuǐ emerges from here,
and flows west into Fú Shuǐ,
in which there is much beautiful jade.
Another three hundred eighty li to the north,
is Zhūyú Mountain,
where much copper and jade are found on its summit,
and many pines and cypresses grow at its base.
The Zhūyú River originates from here,
and flows eastward into the Máo River.
Another three hundred fifty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dūntóu Zhī Shān,
abundant in gold and jade on its summit,
but devoid of grass and trees.
The Máo Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Qiōng Zé,
where many bó mǎ dwell,
with ox tails and white bodies,
a single horn,
and a call that sounds like a human shout.
Further north three hundred fifty li,
there is a mountain called Gōuwúzhīshān,
on its summit there is much jade,
and at its base much copper.
There is a beast here,
its form like a sheep's body with a human face,
its eyes under its armpits,
tiger's teeth and human claws,
its voice like that of an infant,
named Páoxiāo,
it eats people.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Běixiāo,
which has no stones.
On its southern side, there is much green jade,
and on its northern side, there is much jade.
There is a beast here,
whose shape is like a tiger,
but with a white body and a dog's head,
a horse's tail and a boar's bristles,
named Dúyù.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling a crow,
with a human face,
named Qúyú,
which flies by night and hides by day.
Eating it can cure heatstroke.
The Cén River originates here,
and flows eastward into the Qióng Marsh.
Another three hundred fifty li to the north,
there is Mount Liángqú,
with no grasses or trees,
but abundant in metal and jade.
The Xiū River flows from here,
running eastward into Yànmén,
where the beasts are mostly Jūjì,
which resemble hedgehogs but have red fur,
and their sound is like that of a pig.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling Kuāfù,
with four wings, one eye, and a dog's tail,
named Xiāo,
its call is like that of a magpie,
eating it cures abdominal pain,
and it can stop diarrhea.
Another four hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Gūguàn,
with no grass or trees.
This mountain
has snow both in winter and summer.
Further north three hundred eighty li,
is called the Húguàn Mountains,
on its sunny side there is much jade,
on its shady side much green jade,
and many horses.
The Húguàn River flows out from here,
and flows eastward into the sea,
in which there are many eels.
There is a tree here,
whose leaves are like willow with red veins.
Further north, travel five hundred li by water,
then three hundred li through flowing sands,
until reaching Huánshān.
Its summit abounds with gold and jade.
Three mulberry trees grow there,
all of which are without branches,
and stand a hundred ren tall.
A hundred fruit trees flourish there,
while beneath them dwell many strange snakes.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dūntí,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in metal and jade.
It stands by the North Sea.
All the mountains in the Second Scroll of the North,
from Guǎncén Mountain to Dūntí Mountain,
amount to seventeen mountains in total,
spanning five thousand six hundred and ninety li.
Their deities all have serpent bodies and human faces.
The sacrifices to them are as follows:
bury one rooster and one pig as offerings with hair;
use one bi disc and one gui tablet,
and cast them without offering grain.
The first of the "Northern Third Classic" is called the Tàiháng Mountains.
Its beginning is called Guī Mountain,
on its summit there are gold and jade,
and below it there is green jade.
There is a beast here,
its form resembling a antelope but with four horns,
a horse's tail and with spurs,
its name is Hún,
skilled at circling,
its call is its own name.
There is a bird here,
which looks like a magpie,
with a white body, red tail, and six feet,
its name is Bān,
it is easily startled,
and its call sounds like its own name.
Another two hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Lónghóu Zhī Shān,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
The Jué Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Hé.
In its waters dwell many human-fish,
which resemble tí fish in appearance,
have four feet,
and make sounds like infants.
Eating them prevents foolishness and diseases.
Two hundred li further to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Mǎchéngzhīshān.
On its summit, there are many patterned stones,
and on its shady side, abundant metal and jade.
A creature dwells there,
resembling a white dog with a black head,
which takes flight upon seeing humans.
Its name is Tiānmǎ,
and its call echoes its own name.
There is a bird here,
its appearance like a crow,
with a white head, green body, and yellow feet,
named Jūjū,
its call sounds like its name,
eating it prevents hunger,
and it can cure delusions.
Another seventy li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Xián Shān.
On its summit, there is jade,
and at its base, an abundance of copper.
It is rich in pine and cypress trees,
and among the grasses, zǐcǎo is plentiful.
The Tiáo Jiān River originates here,
flowing southwest into Cháng Zé.
In it, there is much qì suān,
which takes three years to form once,
and eating it cures skin diseases.
Further northeast two hundred li,
lies the mountain of Tiānchí,
on which there are no grasses or trees,
but many patterned stones.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a rabbit with a mouse's head,
that flies using its back,
and its name is Fēishǔ.
Miǎnshuǐ emerges from it,
flows hidden beneath it,
and in it there is much yellow chalk.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Yángshān,
on which there is much jade,
and below which there is much gold and copper.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles a cow but has a red tail,
with a lump on its neck,
looking like a ceremonial vessel stand,
named Lǐnghú.
Its call sounds like its own name,
and eating it can cure madness.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a female pheasant,
and is adorned with five colors in patterns,
it naturally combines male and female in itself,
named Xiàngshé,
its call sounds like its name.
The Liú River originates here,
flowing southward to empty into the Yellow River.
In it dwells the Xiànfù fish,
whose shape is like a crucian carp,
with a fish's head and a pig's body,
eating it cures vomiting.
Another three hundred fifty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Bēn Wén,
on its summit much green jade is found,
at its base much yellow chalk,
and abundant alum stone.
Another hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Wángwū,
which is abundant in stones.
The Juān River flows from here,
and runs northwest into the Great Marsh.
Further northeast three hundred li,
is called Jiào Shān,
on which there is much jade but no stone.
Jiào Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing west into the Hé,
this river dries up in winter and flows in summer,
truly a dry river.
Within it are two mountains,
these mountains,
measure three hundred paces in circumference,
their names are Fāwán Zhī Shān,
on them there are gold and jade.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Jǐng Shān.
To the south, one can overlook the marsh of Yán Fàn,
and to the north, Shǎo Zé.
On its summit, there is an abundance of grasses and yams,
among the grasses, many Qin peppers,
on its shady side, much red ochre,
and on its sunny side, much jade.
There is a bird here,
whose form is like a snake,
with four wings, six eyes, and three feet,
named Suān Yǔ.
Its call echoes its own name,
and when it appears, there is fear in the city.
Another three hundred and twenty li to the southeast,
there is Mount Mèngmén,
on its summit abundant gray jade,
much gold, and at its base plentiful yellow chalk,
and ample alum stone.
Another three hundred twenty li to the southeast,
is called Píng Shān.
Píng Shuǐ emerges from its summit,
and submerges beneath it,
where there is much beautiful jade.
Another three hundred li to the east is Jīngshān,
where there is beautiful jade,
abundant lacquer trees,
and plentiful bamboo.
On its southern side, there is red copper,
and on its northern side, there is black whetstone.
The Gāo River originates here,
flowing south into the Hé River.
Two hundred li further east,
stands Chóngwěi Mountain,
rich in metal and jade on its summit,
abundant with bamboo at its base,
and plentiful in green jasper.
Dān River originates here,
flowing south into the Yellow River.
Bó River also springs forth,
and southeastward flows into Huáng Marsh.
Another three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Péngpí Zhī Shān,
on which there are no grasses or trees,
but much metal and jade,
and at its foot, much water.
The Zǎolín River flows out from here,
running southeast and emptying into the Hé River.
The Féi River also flows out from here,
and runs south to empty into the Chuáng River,
in which there are many féiyí snakes.
Another hundred eighty li to the east,
lies Mount Xiǎohóu.
The Míngzhāng River originates here,
flowing south into Huángzé.
There is a bird here,
whose form resembles a crow but with white patterns,
named Gūxí,
and eating it prevents drunkenness.
Another three hundred seventy li to the east,
there is Mount Tàitóu,
from which the Gòng River originates,
flowing south into the Hūtuó River.
On its summit, there is an abundance of metal and jade,
and at its base, many bamboo arrows grow.
Further northeast two hundred li,
lies Xuānyuán Mountain,
on its summit there is much copper,
and at its foot, abundant bamboo.
There is a bird here,
its form resembling an owl with a white head,
its name is Huángniǎo,
its call echoes its own name,
and eating it prevents jealousy.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Yèlìzhīshān,
on which grow many pines and cypresses,
and where metal and jade are found.
The Qìnshuǐ River originates here,
flowing southward into the Hé River.
To its east, there is a forest,
named Dānlín.
The waters of Dānlín originate here,
flowing southward into the Hé River.
The Yīnghóuzhīshuǐ River originates here,
flowing northward into the Fànshuǐ River.
Three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Jùrùzhīshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
but containing metal and jade.
The Jì Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing southward into the Hé.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Shénqūnzhīshān.
On its summit, there are patterned stones;
at its base, white snakes dwell,
and there are flying insects.
The Huángshuǐ River originates here,
flowing eastward into the Huán River.
The Fǔshuǐ River also springs from this mountain,
running east to join the Ōushuǐ River.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Fājiūzhīshān,
on which grow many mulberry trees.
There is a bird there,
whose shape resembles a crow,
with a patterned head, white beak, and red feet,
named Jīngwèi,
whose call is its own name.
She was the youngest daughter of Emperor Yán, named Nǚwá.
Nǚwá went swimming in the Eastern Sea,
drowned and did not return.
Therefore, she became Jīngwèi,
often carrying twigs and stones from the Western Mountains,
to fill up the Eastern Sea.
The Zhāng River originates there,
flowing eastward into the Hé River.
Another hundred and twenty li to the northeast,
there is Shǎo Shān,
on which there are metal and jade,
and beneath it, there is copper.
The Qīng Zhāng River originates from here,
flowing east into the Zhuó Zhāng River.
Another two hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Xī Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and at its foot lies whetstone.
The Niúshǒu River originates from here,
and flows eastward into the Fǔ River.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Jǐngshān,
which contains beautiful jade.
The Jǐngshuǐ River originates from it,
flowing southeast into the Hǎizé Marsh.
Another hundred li north,
there is a mountain called Tíshǒu,
where jade is found,
abundant in stones
but without water.
Another hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Xiù,
on which there are jade and green jasper.
Its trees are mostly Xún,
and its plants are mostly Sháoyào and Xiōngqióng.
The Wèi River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into the Yellow River.
In it, there are Hù and Měng.
Another hundred and twenty li to the north,
there is Mount Sōng.
The Yáng River flows out from here,
running northeast and emptying into the Hé River.
Another one hundred and twenty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Dūnyǔ,
on which there are no grasses or trees,
but there are metal and jade.
The Suò River originates from its southern side,
and flows eastward into the waters of Tàilù.
The Zhī River originates from its northern side,
and flows eastward into the Péng River.
The Huái River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into the Zhī Marsh.
Another hundred seventy li to the north,
is Zhèshān,
where its southern side has gold and jade,
and its northern side has iron.
The Lìjù River originates from here,
and flows north into the Wěishuǐ River.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Wéilóng.
On its summit there is green jade,
on its southern side there is gold,
and on its northern side there is iron.
The Féi River flows out from here,
and runs eastward into the Gāo Marsh,
in which there are many piled-up rocks.
The Chǎngtiě River flows out from here,
and runs northward into the Great Marsh.
Another one hundred eighty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Báimǎ Zhī Shān.
On its southern side, there is an abundance of stone and jade,
while on its northern side, there is much iron,
as well as plenty of red copper.
The Mùmǎ River originates from here,
and flows northeast to empty into the Hūtuó River.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Kōngsāng,
with no grass or trees,
and snow in both winter and summer.
The Wǎngsāng River originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Hūtuó River.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Tàixì Zhī Shān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in metal and jade.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles a sheep,
with one horn and one eye,
the eye located behind the ear,
named Dōngdōng.
Its call sounds like its own name.
The Hūtuó River originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Lóu River.
The Yènǚ River emerges from its southern side,
flowing southward into the Qìn River.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Shí Shān,
rich in deposits of gold and jade.
The Huòhuò River originates here,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Hūtuó River.
The Xiānyú River also originates here,
flowing southward and emptying into the Hūtuó River.
Another two hundred li to the north,
lies Tóngróng Mountain.
Gāotú River originates from here,
and flows eastward into Lóuyè River.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Gāoshì.
The Zī River flows out of it
and runs south before emptying into the Hūtuó River.
Its trees are mostly palms,
and its grasses are mostly willows.
The Kòu River flows out of it
and runs east before emptying into the Yellow River.
Another three hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Lùshān,
abundant with fine jade.
The Jiāngshuǐ River originates from here,
and flows eastward
into the Hé River.
Another two hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Yí Shān.
Bān Shuǐ originates from it,
and flows eastward into the Hé.
One hundred twenty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Yànshān,
which abounds in Yīng stones.
The Yàn River flows from here,
running eastward and emptying into the Hé River.
Traveling northward five hundred li by land,
and five hundred li by water,
one arrives at Ráo Shān.
This mountain has no grass or trees,
but abounds in yáo and jade stones,
with many tuótuó among its beasts,
and numerous liú among its birds.
The Lìguó River originates here,
flowing eastward into the Hé.
In it dwells the shī fish,
which, if eaten, can kill a person.
Another four hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Qián Shān.
It has no grass or trees,
with metal and jade on its southern side,
and iron but no water on its northern side.
There is a beast there,
shaped like an ox but with three legs,
named Yuán,
whose call sounds like its own name.
Another five hundred li to the north,
there is a mountain called Lún Shān.
The Lún River flows out from it,
and runs eastward into the Yellow River.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles that of a river deer,
with its anus located on its tail,
and its name is Pí Jiǔ.
Another five hundred li to the north,
there is Mount Jiéshí.
Shéng Shuǐ originates from it,
and flows eastward into the Hé,
in which there are many Púyí fish.
On its summit there is jade,
and at its base much green jasper.
Then, traveling five hundred li north by water,
one arrives at Yànmén Mountain,
where there are no grasses or trees.
Then northward by water for four hundred li,
one reaches the Great Marsh.
There is a mountain in it,
called Dìdū Mountain,
which spans a hundred li in circumference,
with no grass or trees,
but containing metal and jade.
Further north five hundred li,
there is a mountain called Chúnyú Wúféng Zhī Shān.
To the north, one gazes upon Jīhào Zhī Shān,
where the wind blows like a sharp gale;
to the west, one looks at Yōudū Zhī Shān,
from which the Yù Shuǐ River flows.
Here dwells a great serpent,
with a red head and white body,
whose sound is like that of an ox.
When it appears, the region suffers a great drought.
All of the first mountains in the "Third Collection of the Northern Mountains,"
from Tàiháng Zhī Shān to Wúféng Zhī Shān,
amount to forty-six mountains in total,
spanning twelve thousand three hundred and fifty li.
Among the deities, twenty have the form of
horse bodies with human faces.
When sacrificing to them,
one uses an algae and chǎi plant, burying it.
Fourteen of the deities
have the form of pig bodies adorned with jade.
When sacrificing to them,
only jade is used,
and it is not buried.
Ten of the deities
have the form of pig bodies with eight legs
and snake tails.
When sacrificing to them,
one uses a bi disc, burying it.
In total, there are forty-four deities,
and all are sacrificed to with glutinous rice offerings,
none of which are cooked with fire.
The Records of the Mountains in the Northern Classic,
in total comprise eighty-seven mountains,
spanning twenty-three thousand two hundred and thirty li.
The first mountain in the Classic of the Eastern Mountains,
is called Sùzhū Zhī Shān.
To the north, it overlooks Gānmèi.
The Shí Shuǐ originates from here,
and flows northeast into the sea.
In it, there are many Yōngyōng fish,
which have the appearance of犁牛(lí niú, a type of cattle),
and make a sound like the grunting of a pig.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Lěi Shān,
on its summit there is jade,
and at its base there is gold.
The Hú Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing eastward into the Shí Shuǐ,
and in it there are many tadpoles.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is Mount Xúnzhuàng,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and below it there is much green jade stone.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a dog,
with six feet,
named Cóngcóng,
and its call is its own name.
There is a bird here,
shaped like a chicken but with rat-like fur,
named Zīshǔ,
whose appearance causes great drought in the city.
The Zhī River flows out from here,
and flows north into Lake Water.
In it there are many Zhēn fish,
