shaped like Tiáo fish,
with beaks like needles,
and eating them prevents epidemic diseases.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Bóqí,
with no grass or trees,
and no water.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Fāntiáo Zhī Shān,
with no grass or trees,
and much sand.
Jiǎn Shuǐ flows from here,
running northward into the sea,
and in it, there are many gǎn fish.
Another four hundred li to the south,
stands Mount Gū'ér,
where lacquer trees abound on its summit,
and mulberry and paper mulberry trees flourish at its base.
The Gū'ér River originates from here,
flowing northward into the sea,
and within its waters, many elopichthys bambusa fish thrive.
Another four hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Gāoshìzhī Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and at its foot, many needle stones.
The Zhūshéng River originates here,
flowing eastward into a marsh,
where there is an abundance of gold and jade.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Yuè Shān,
on which there are many mulberry trees,
and at its foot, many ailanthus trees.
Luò Shuǐ originates from here,
flows eastward into a marsh,
and in it, there is much gold and jade.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Chái Shān.
Its summit has no grasses or trees,
and at its base, there is much water.
In it dwell many fish called kān xù.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles Kuāfù but with bristles like a pig,
its cry sounds like a shout,
and when it appears, there will be great floods under heaven.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Dú Shān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and below it there are many beautiful stones.
The Mòtú River flows out from here,
and runs southeast into the Miǎn River.
In it there are many Tiáoyǒng creatures,
which have the form of yellow snakes,
with fish-like fins,
and emit light when they come in and out of the water.
When they appear,
the city will suffer a great drought.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is Mount Tài,
on which there is much jade,
and beneath which there is much gold.
There is a beast here,
whose form is like a suckling pig but has pearls,
named Tóngtóng,
its name comes from its own call.
The Huán River flows out from here,
running eastward into the river,
in which there is much crystal.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Zhúshān,
which stands by the river,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in yáo and bì jade.
The Jī Shuǐ originates from here,
and flows southeast into the Qǔtán Zhī Shuǐ,
where there are many zǐluó snails.
All of the first mountains in the "Eastern Mountains Classic,"
from the Sùzhū Mountains to the Zhú Mountains,
amount to twelve mountains in total,
spanning three thousand six hundred lǐ.
Their deities all have human bodies and dragon heads.
For sacrifices: use the hair of one dog for prayer,
and use fish for the ear ceremony.
The first mountain in the Book of Regions: East II,
is called Kōngsāng Mountain.
It borders the Shí River to the north,
overlooks Jūwú to the east,
looks upon Shālíng to the south,
and faces Mǐnzé to the west.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox with tiger stripes,
whose sound resembles a moan,
named Línglíng.
Its call echoes its own name,
and when it appears, great floods will sweep the land.
Another six hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Cáoxī Zhī Shān,
below which there are many paper mulberry trees but no water,
and many birds and beasts.
Another four hundred li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Yìgāo Zhī Shān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and at its base, an abundance of white chalk.
The Yìgāo River flows from here,
running eastward into the Jīnǚ River,
where there are many clams and pearl oysters.
Then, heading south by water for five hundred li,
crossing three hundred li of flowing sands,
one arrives at the tail of Gè Shān.
There are no grasses or trees,
but abundant whetstones.
Another three hundred eighty li to the south,
is called the beginning of Gé Shān,
with no grass or trees.
Lǐ Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing eastward into Yú Zé,
in which there are many zhū biē yú,
shaped like lungs with four eyes,
six legs and possessing pearls,
their flavor sour and sweet,
eating them prevents pestilence.
Further south three hundred eighty *li*,
there is a mountain called Yú'ézhī Shān,
on its upper parts grow many catalpa and nanmu trees,
while its lower parts are covered with brambles and millet.
The Záyú River originates here,
flowing eastward into the Huángshuǐ River.
There is a beast dwelling here,
whose form resembles a rabbit but with a bird's beak,
owl eyes and a snake's tail.
When it sees people, it feigns sleep,
and is named Qíyú.
Its call is the sound of its own name,
and when it appears, locusts and grasshoppers will cause crop damage.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Dùfù,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant water.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Gěng Shān,
with no grass or trees,
abundant in crystal,
and many large snakes.
There is a beast there,
shaped like a fox but with fish-like fins,
named Zhū Rú,
whose call sounds like its own name,
and when it appears, the state it is in will experience fear.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Lúqízhī Shān,
with no grass or trees,
abundant in sand and stones.
Shā Shuǐ originates from here,
flows southward, and empties into Cén Shuǐ,
where there are many lìhú birds,
which resemble mandarin ducks but have human feet,
their call sounds like their own name,
and when they appear, it means the state will have many earthwork projects.
Another three hundred eighty li to the south,
there is a mountain called Gūyèzhīshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
with abundant water.
Again, going south by water for three hundred li,
through a hundred li of flowing sands,
there is a mountain called Běi Gūshè Zhī Shān,
with no grasses or trees,
and many rocks.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Nángūshè,
devoid of grass and trees,
but abundant in water.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Bìshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
abounding in large snakes,
and plentiful in green jade.
Another five hundred li to the south,
there is Mount Gōushì,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
Yuán Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing eastward into Shā Zé.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Gūféng,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a fox but with wings,
its call resembling that of a wild goose,
named Bìbì.
When it appears, there will be a great drought throughout the land.
Another five hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Fúlìzhīshān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and at its foot much needle stone.
There is a beast here,
whose form is like a fox,
but with nine tails,
nine heads,
and tiger claws,
named Lóngzhì,
its cry is like that of a baby,
and it eats people.
Another five hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Yōu Shān,
facing the Yōu River to the south,
and overlooking a lake to the east.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a horse,
with sheep's eyes,
four horns,
and an ox's tail.
Its cry resembles that of a howling dog,
and its name is Yóu Yóu.
When it appears, the state will have many cunning people.
There is a bird here,
shaped like a wild duck but with a rat's tail,
adept at climbing trees.
Its name is Jié Gōu,
and when it appears, the state will suffer many epidemics.
The beginning of the "Second Classic of the Eastern Mountains" records,
from the Kōngsāng Mountains to the Zhé Mountain,
a total of seventeen mountains,
spanning six thousand six hundred and forty li.
The deities here all have beast-like bodies, human faces, and wear antlers.
For their sacrifices:
use one chicken as a fur offering in prayer,
and bury one jade disc as an infant offering.
Furthermore, the first mountain of the Eastern Third Range,
is called Shīhú Zhī Shān.
To the north, one gazes upon Xiāng Shān.
On its heights, there is much metal and jade,
and below it, many thorny bushes.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a river deer but with fish-like eyes,
named Wǎn Hú,
whose call is its own name.
Then, traveling eight hundred li south by water,
one arrives at Qí Shān.
Its trees are mostly peach and plum,
and its beasts are mostly tigers.
Then, traveling five hundred li south by water,
one arrives at Zhūgōu Mountain,
where there is no grass or trees,
but much sand and stone.
This mountain,
spanning a hundred li in breadth,
abounds in sleeper fish.
Again, traveling seven hundred lǐ south by water,
one reaches Mount Zhōngfù,
which has no grasses or trees,
and is covered with much sand.
Again eastward by water for a thousand leagues,
there is a mountain called Húshèzhī,
with no grasses or trees,
but abundant sand and stones.
Further south, traveling seven hundred li by water,
there is a mountain called Mèngzǐ.
Its trees are mostly catalpa and tung,
with many peach and plum trees,
its grasses abundant in mushrooms and rushes,
and its beasts mostly elk and deer.
This mountain,
spans a hundred li in breadth.
On its summit, water emerges,
named Bìyáng,
in which there are many sturgeon and Chinese sturgeon.
Then, traveling five hundred li south by water,
there is a place called Flowing Sands.
After journeying five hundred li,
there stands a mountain,
named Qǐzhǒng Mountain.
It spans two hundred li in circumference,
with no grasses or trees,
but inhabited by large snakes,
and abundant jade on its summit.
There is a body of water there,
covering forty li in circumference, all surging,
named Shēnzé.
Within it dwell many hawksbill turtles.
There is a fish there,
shaped like a carp,
but with six feet and a bird's tail,
named Gégé Fish,
whose call echoes its own name.
Then traveling south by water for nine hundred li,
one arrives at Mǔyú Mountain,
where plants and trees grow on its summit,
abundant in metal and jade,
and rich in red ochre.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox with a horse's tail,
named Jīngjīng,
whose call echoes its own name.
Then, heading south by water for five hundred li,
crossing three hundred li of flowing sands,
one arrives at Wúgāo Mountain.
To the south, one gazes upon the Young Sea,
and to the east, upon the Fusang Tree.
There are no grasses or trees,
and it is often windy.
This mountain
spreads across an area of a hundred li in circumference.
All of the mountains in the third book of the Eastern Mountains,
from Shīhú Zhī Shān to Wúgāo Zhī Shān,
amount to nine mountains,
spanning six thousand nine hundred li.
The spirits there all have human bodies with ram's horns.
For their sacrifices:
use one male sheep,
and millet for the grain offering.
These spirits,
when they appear, bring wind and rain that cause ruin.
Again, the first mountain of the Eastern Fourth Range,
is called Běihào Zhī Shān,
overlooking the North Sea.
There is a tree there,
its shape like a poplar,
with red blossoms,
its fruit like a jujube but without a pit,
its taste sour and sweet,
eating it prevents malaria.
The Shí Shuǐ emerges from there,
and flows northeast into the sea.
There is a beast there,
its shape like a wolf,
with a red head and rat-like eyes,
its cry like a pig,
named Gédá,
it eats people.
There is a bird there,
its shape like a chicken with a white head,
rat-like feet and tiger claws,
its name is Qíquè,
it also eats people.
Another three hundred li to the south,
there is a mountain called Máo Shān,
with no grass or trees.
The Cāngtǐ River originates here,
and flows west into the Zhǎn River.
In it, there are many Xiū fish,
which resemble carp but have large heads.
Those who eat them will not get warts.
Another three hundred twenty li to the south,
there is a mountain called Dōngshǐzhī Shān,
on which there is much gray jade.
There is a tree here,
its shape like a poplar but with red grain,
its sap like blood,
it bears no fruit,
its name is Qǐ,
and it can be used to tame horses.
The Cǐ River flows out from here,
and runs northeast to pour into the sea,
in which there are many beautiful shells,
and many Zǐ fish,
whose shape is like a crucian carp,
with one head and ten bodies,
their odor like that of Míwú,
and eating them prevents flatulence.
Another three hundred li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Nǚzhēngzhīshān,
on which there are no grasses or trees.
The Shígāo River flows from here,
and runs westward into the Gé River.
In it, there are many Bóyú fish,
which look like sturgeon but have only one eye,
and make a sound like retching.
When they appear, there will be a great drought throughout the land.
Another two hundred li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Qīn Shān,
abundant in metal and jade but lacking in stone.
The Shī Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing northward into Gāo Zé,
where there are many xiū fish
and patterned shells.
There is a beast here;
it looks like a pig but has tusks,
and its name is Dāngkāng.
It calls out its own name,
and when it appears, the world will enjoy a great harvest.
Another two hundred li to the southeast,
is Mount Zǐtóng.
The Zǐtóng River flows out from here;
and runs westward into the Rúyé Marsh.
In it, there are many huá fish,
which look like fish but have bird wings,
emit light when they surface or dive,
and sound like mandarin ducks.
Their appearance foretells a great drought in the world.
Further northeast two hundred li,
there is a mountain called Shàn Shān,
abundant in metal and jade.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a pig with a human face,
yellow body and red tail,
its name is Héyǔ,
its cry resembles that of an infant.
This beast,
eats humans,
and also consumes insects and snakes,
its appearance heralds great floods across the land.
Another two hundred li to the east,
stands Mount Tài,
on which there are abundant metals and jade,
as well as zhēn trees.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ox with a white head,
one eye and a snake's tail,
named Fěi.
Wherever it walks through water, the water dries up;
wherever it treads on grass, the grass dies.
Its appearance heralds a great plague throughout the land.
The Gōu River originates here,
flowing northward into the Láo River,
and in it dwell many xū fish.
The first mountain of the "Fourth Classic of the Eastern Mountains,"
ranges from the Běihào Mountain to the Great Mountain,
comprising a total of eight mountains,
spanning one thousand seven hundred and twenty li.
This concludes the record of the mountains in the Eastern Classic,
comprising forty-six mountains in total,
spanning eighteen thousand eight hundred and sixty li.
The first mountain of the Bó Shān range,
is called Gān Zǎo Zhī Shān.
The Gòng Shuǐ originates here,
and flows west into the Hé.
On its summit, there is an abundance of niǔ trees,
and below it, there is a grass,
with a sunflower-like root and apricot-like leaves,
yellow flowers and pod-like fruits,
named Tuò,
which can be used to cure eye conditions.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a húan rat with a patterned forehead,
named Nuó,
and eating it can cure goiters.
Another twenty li to the east,
there is Lì'ér Mountain,
on which there are many oak trees,
and many lì trees.
This kind of tree
has a square stem and round leaves,
yellow flowers with fuzz,
and its fruit resembles that of the chinaberry tree.
If one consumes it, one will not forget.
Another fifteen li to the east,
is called the Qúzhū Mountains,
where bamboos abound on its summit.
The Qúzhū River originates from there,
and flows southward into the Yellow River.
In it are many Háo fish,
shaped like the wěi fish,
with red beaks, red tails, and red fins,
and eating them can cure white ringworm.
Another thirty-five li to the east,
there is Mount Cōnglóng,
within which are many great valleys,
and an abundance of white chalk,
black, green,
and yellow chalk.
Another fifteen li to the east,
there is a mountain called Wō Shān,
on which there is much red copper,
and on its shady side, much iron.
Another seventy li to the east,
there is a mountain called Tuòhù.
There is a plant there,
shaped like sunflower leaves with red flowers,
bearing pods,
the seeds of which resemble palm nuts,
named Zhíchǔ.
It can be used to cure tumors,
and eating it prevents nightmares.
Twenty li further to the east,
there is a mountain called Jīnxīng,
abundant with tiānyīng plants,
which resemble dragon bones in appearance,
and can be used to cure boils.
Another seventy li to the east,
there is Mount Tàiwēi,
within which lies a valley called Xiāo Valley,
where there is an abundance of iron.
Another fifteen li to the east,
stands the Jiānggǔ Mountain,
rich in red copper within it.
Another hundred and twenty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Wúlín,
where much jiān grass grows.
Another thirty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Niúshǒu.
There is a plant there,
named guǐcǎo,
whose leaves resemble those of the sunflower but with red stems,
and whose blooms look like grain.
Consuming it dispels worries.
The Láo River originates here,
flowing westward into the Jué River.
Here, there are many flying fish,
which resemble crucian carp in appearance,
and eating them cures hemorrhoids and diarrhea.
Another forty li to the north,
there is Mount Huò,
where the trees are mostly paper mulberries.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles a wildcat,
but with a white tail and a mane,
named Fěifěi.
Raising it can dispel melancholy.
Another fifty-two li to the north,
there is a mountain called Hégǔ Zhī Shān,
where many zhānjí plants grow.
Another thirty-five li to the north,
there is a mountain called Yīnshān,
with abundant whetstones
and patterned stones.
Shǎoshuǐ River originates from here,
where many diāotáng trees grow.
Their leaves resemble elm leaves but are square in shape,
and their fruits look like red beans.
Eating them can cure deafness.
Further northeast four hundred li,
there is a mountain called Gǔdèng Zhī Shān,
rich in red copper.
There is a plant here,
named róngcǎo,
its leaves like willow,
its root like a chicken egg,
eating it cures rheumatism.
The first mountain range of the Bó group,
stretches from Gānzǎo Mountain to Gǔdēng Mountain,
comprising fifteen mountains in total,
spanning six thousand six hundred and seventy li.
Lì'ér Mountain
is the ancestral peak,
and the sacrificial rites are as follows:
The animal offerings consist of a full set of the Great Sacrifice;
and auspicious jade is suspended.
For the remaining thirteen mountains,
the animal offering is a single sheep,
with mulberry tokens hung as pendants,
buried without the use of sacrificial rice.
The mulberry tokens
are mulberry spirit tablets,
square at the base and pointed at the top,
pierced through the center and adorned with metal.
The first mountain of the Jìshān range in the Central Second Classic,
is called Huīzhūzhī Shān.
On its summit grows abundant mulberry,
its beasts are mostly wild donkeys and elk,
and its birds are mostly pheasants.
Again two hundred li to the southwest,
there is a mountain called Fāshì.
On its summit there is much metal and jade,
and at its base there are many whetstones.
The Jíyú River flows out from here,
and runs west to empty into the Yī River.
Three hundred li further to the west,
there is a mountain called Háo Shān.
On its summit, there is an abundance of metal and jade, but no grasses or trees.
Three hundred li further to the west,
there is a mountain called Xiān Shān,
abundant in metal and jade,
but devoid of grass and trees.
The Xiān Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing northward and emptying into the Yī Shuǐ.
In it, there are many míng shé,
which have the form of snakes but with four wings,
and their sound is like that of a chime stone.
When they appear, the region will suffer a great drought.
Three hundred li further west,
there is Yángshān,
which has many rocks,
but no grass or trees.
Yángshuǐ originates from it,
and flows north into the Yīshuǐ.
In it, there are many Huàshé,
whose form is like a human face with a jackal's body,
bird wings and a snake's movement,
their sound is like scolding or shouting,
and when they appear, the city will have a great flood.
Two hundred li further west,
there is Mount Kūnwú,
on which there is much red copper.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a pig but with horns,
its cry sounds like a howl,
named Lóngzhì,
and eating it will prevent nightmares.
Another hundred twenty miles to the west,
there is Jiān Mountain.
The Jiān River flows out from here,
and runs northward into the Yi River.
On its heights there is much metal and jade,
and at its base there is much green and red orpiment.
There is a tree here,
whose shape is like a pear tree but with red leaves,
named máng grass,
which can be used to poison fish.
Another one hundred fifty miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Dúsū,
which has no grasses or trees but abundant water.
Two hundred li further to the west,
there is a mountain called Mànqúzhīshān.
On its summit, there is an abundance of metal and jade,
while at its base, there are many bamboo arrows.
The Yīshuǐ River originates here,
flowing eastward and emptying into the Luò River.
There is a beast dwelling there,
whose name is Mǎfù.
It has the appearance of a human face on a tiger's body,
and its cry resembles that of an infant.
It is a man-eater.
The first chapter of the Classic of the Jì Mountains,
from the Huīzhū Mountains to the Mànqú Mountains,
covers a total of nine mountains,
spanning one thousand six hundred and seventy lǐ.
Their deities all have human faces and bird bodies.
For sacrifices, use hairy animals,
employ one auspicious jade,
and cast it without offering grain.
The first mountain of the Fù Shān range in the Central Third Classic,
is called Áo Àn Zhī Shān.
Its sunny side abounds with Tūfú jade,
and its shady side has plenty of ochre
and gold.
The spirit Xūn Chí resides there.
It often produces beautiful jade.
Looking north, one sees the river forests,
their appearance like madder or like raised objects.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles a white deer with four horns,
named Fū Zhū,
and when it appears, the city will experience great floods.
Another ten li to the east,
is the mountain called Qīngyào,
which truly serves as the secret capital of the Emperor.
To the north, one gazes upon the bends of the Yellow River,
where many Jià birds are found.
To the south, one looks upon Shànzhǔ,
the place where Yǔ's father transformed,
and there are many Púléi
and Púlú.
Shén Wǔluó governs it,
whose form is a human face with leopard patterns,
a slender waist and white teeth,
and ears pierced with earrings,
its call resembling the sound of jade chiming.
This mountain
is beneficial for women.
The Zhěn River flows out from here,
and runs northward to empty into the Yellow River.
In it, there is a bird,
named Yāo,
which looks like a wild duck,
with a green body, red eyes, and a crimson tail,
and eating it is beneficial for fertility.
There is a grass here,
resembling jiān,
with a square stem, yellow flowers, and red fruit,
its root like gǎoběn,
named Xún grass,
and consuming it beautifies one's complexion.
Another ten li to the east,
there is a mountain called Guīshān,
on which there grow fine jujubes,
and on its northern side, there is jade of the Túfú kind.
The Zhènghuí River originates from here,
flowing northward into the Yellow River.
In it, there are many flying fish,
which look like pigs with red patterns.
Eating them makes one unafraid of thunder,
and it can ward off weapons.
Forty li further east,
stands the Yísū Mountain,
abundant with metals and jade on its summit,
and covered with蔓居 trees at its base.
The Yōngyǒng River flows from here,
running northward to empty into the Yellow River,
where many yellow shells are found.
Twenty li further to the east,
there is Héshān.
Its summit has no grasses or trees but is rich in yáo jade and green jade,
and it truly serves as the convergence point of the nine tributaries of the Hé River.
This mountain winds in five bends,
from which nine rivers emerge,
converge and flow northward into the Hé River,
and within it, there is an abundance of dark green jade.
The auspicious spirit Tàiféng presides over it,
whose form resembles a human but with a tiger's tail,
and who prefers to dwell on the southern side of Fùshān,
emanating light upon entry and exit.
Tàiféng has the power to stir the energies of heaven and earth.
Of the first range of Fù Mountains,
from Mount Ào'àn to Mount Héshān,
there are altogether five mountains,
spanning four hundred and forty li.
For the sacrifices to Tàiféng,
Xūnchí,
and Wǔluó, a single ram is used and split open,
with auspicious jade offered as pendants.
For the other two deities, a single rooster is buried as a sacrifice,
using polished rice as the offering grain.
The first mountain of the Lí Shān range in the Central Fourth Classic,
is called Lùtí Zhī Shān.
On its summit, there is an abundance of jade,
and at its base, much gold.
The Gān Shuǐ originates here,
flowing northward into the Luò River,
and within it, there are many gàn stones.
Fifty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Fúzhū,
on which there are many jade-like stones.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a badger but with human eyes,
and its name is Yín.
The Guó River originates here,
flowing northward into the Luò River,
and in it are many colorful stones.
Another one hundred twenty li to the west,
there is Lí Shān.
On its southern side, there is much jade,
and on its northern side, much sow thistle.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles an ox,
with a bluish body,
and its cry is like that of an infant.
It eats people,
and its name is Xīqú.
The Yōngyōng River flows out from here,
and flows south into the Yī River.
There is another beast here,
named Jié,
whose form is like a snarling dog but has scales,
and its fur is like the bristles of a pig.
Another two hundred li to the west,
there is Mount Jīwěi,
abundant with paper mulberry trees,
rich in ochre stones,
and on its summit, much Túfú jade.
Two hundred and fifty li further west,
there is a mountain called Bǐng Shān.
Its summit is rich in jade,
and its foothills abound in copper.
The Tāodiāo River originates here,
flowing northward into the Luò River.
In it dwell many qián yáng.
There is a tree here,
whose shape resembles the chū tree,
with leaves like the tóng tree and pod-like fruits,
named bá,
which can be used to poison fish.
Two hundred li further west,
there is a mountain called Báibiānzhīshān,
on which there is abundant metal and jade,
and at its base, plenty of azurite and orpiment.
Another two hundred li to the west,
stands Xióng'ěr Mountain,
abundant with lacquer trees on its summit,
and palms at its base.
The Fúláo River originates here,
flowing westward into the Luò River,
rich in crystal within its waters,
and teeming with mermaids.
There is a plant there,
resembling perilla but with red blossoms,
named Tíngníng,
which can be used to poison fish.
Another three hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Mǔ Shān,
on which there is much patterned stone,
and below it many arrow bamboos
and bamboo mèi.
Among the animals, there are many zuò oxen
and qián yáng,
and among the birds, many red bì.
Three hundred fifty li further west,
there is a mountain called Huānjǔ.
The Luò River flows out from here,
and runs northeast into the Xuānhù River.
In it are many horse-intestine-like creatures.
These two mountains
are within the Luò region.
All the mountains in the Lí range,
from Lùtí Mountain to Xuánhù Mountain,
span nine mountains in total,
covering one thousand six hundred and seventy li.
Their deities all have human faces and beast bodies.
When offering sacrifices to them,
use a white chicken with its feathers,
pray without offering grain,
and adorn it with colorful silk.
The first mountain of the Bó Shān range in the Central Fifth Classic,
is called Gǒu Chuáng Zhī Shān.
It has no grasses or trees,
but is rich in strange rocks.
Three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Shǒu Shān.
On its northern side, there are many paper mulberry and oak trees,
and among the grasses, many zhú and yuán plants.
On its southern side, there is much jade of the tūfú kind,
and among the trees, many locust trees.
On its northern side, there is a valley,
called Jī Gǔ,
where there are many dì birds.
They look like owls but have three eyes
and ears.
Their sound is like that of a deer,
and eating them will cure dampness diseases.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Xiànzhú Zhī Shān,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in patterned stones.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Cōnglóng,
devoid of grass and trees,
and abundant in bàng stones.
Five hundred li to the northeast,
there is Mount Tiáogǔ,
where the trees are mostly pagoda trees and tung trees,
and the grasses are mostly peonies and
asparagus.
Another ten li to the north,
there is a mountain called Chāo Shān.
On its northern side, there is much green jade,
while on its southern side, there is a well
that has water in winter but dries up in summer.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Chénghóu,
on which there is much varnish tree wood,
and the grass is mostly péng.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Cháogē,
whose valleys abound in fine chalk.
Another five hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Huái Shān,
in whose valleys there is much gold and tin.
Another ten li to the east,
there is Lì Shān,
where the trees are mostly locust trees,
and on its sunny side, there is much jade.
Another ten li to the east,
there is Mount Shī,
abundant with green jade,
and its beasts are mostly river deer.
The Shǐ River flows out from here,
running southward into the Luò River,
and within it lies much fine jade.
Another ten li to the east,
there is Mount Liángyú,
on which there are many paper mulberry trees and oak trees,
but no rocks.
The Yú River originates from its northern side,
and flows north into the Yellow River;
the Rǔ River originates from its southern side,
and flows southeast into the Luò River.
Another ten lǐ to the southeast,
there is Gǔwěi Mountain,
abundant in whetstones
and red copper.
Lóngyú River originates here,
flowing southeast
and emptying into the Luò River.
Further northeast twenty li,
there is a mountain called Shēng Shān,
its trees are mostly paper mulberry, oak, and jujube,
its grasses are mostly yam and thoroughwort,
with abundant kou tuo plants.
The Huáng Suān River originates here,
flowing northward into the Yellow River,
in which there is much fine jade.
Another twelve li to the east,
there is Mount Yángxū,
rich in metal,
overlooking the waters of Xuánhù.
Of the first range of the Bó Mountains,
from the Gǒulín Mountains to the Yángxū Mountains,
there are sixteen mountains in total,
spanning two thousand nine hundred and eighty-two lǐ.
The Shēng Mountain
is the ancestral burial mound.
The sacrificial rites for it:
offer the Tàiláo sacrifice,
and adorn the offerings with auspicious jade.
The Shǒu Mountain
is a divine site,
its sacrifices use rice,
a black sacrificial animal,
the implements for the Tàiláo sacrifice,
and fermented liquor;
perform the shield dance,
set up drums;
and adorn with one jade disc.
The Shī River
connects with heaven,
sacrifice to it with a plump animal,
using one black dog above,
and one hen below,
cut a ewe,
and offer its blood.
Adorn with auspicious jade,
decorate it with colors,
and present it as an offering.
The first mountain of the Gǎodī mountain range in the Central Sixth Classic,
is called Píngféng Mountain.
To the south, one gazes upon the Yī and Luò rivers,
and to the east, upon Gǔchéng Mountain.
It has no grass or trees,
and its waters are abundant with sand and stones.
There is a deity there,
whose form resembles a human but with two heads,
named Jiāochóng.
This is the stinging insect,
and indeed serves as the abode for bees and honey.
For sacrificing to it:
use one rooster,
perform an exorcism but do not kill it.
Ten miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Gǎodīzhīshān,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
Another ten li to the west,
there is a mountain called Guīshān.
On its northern side, there is an abundance of Túfú jade.
To its west, there is a valley,
named Guàngǔ,
where the trees are mostly willows and paper mulberries.
Among them, there is a bird,
shaped like a mountain pheasant but with a long tail,
red as cinnabar flames and with a blue beak,
named Língyāo; its call sounds like its own name,
and wearing its feathers prevents nightmares.
The Jiāoshāng River
originates from its southern side,
and flows south into the Luò River;
the Yúsuí River originates from its northern side,
and flows north into the Gǔshuǐ River.
Another thirty li to the west,
there is a mountain called Zhānzhū.
On its southern side, there is much metal,
and on its northern side, there are many patterned stones. The Xiè River flows from here,
running southeast and emptying into the Luò River;
the Shǎo River arises on its northern side,
and flows east to empty into the Gǔ River.
Another thirty li to the west,
there is Mount Lóuzhuō,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
The Zhān River originates from its southern side,
flowing eastward into the Luò River;
the Bēi River springs from its northern side,
flowing northward into the Gǔ River,
where there are abundant purple stones
and patterned stones.
Another forty li to the west,
there is Mount Báishí.
The Huì River originates from its southern side,
flows southward, and empties into the Luò River,
where there is an abundance of crystal.
The Jiàn River originates from its northern side,
flows northwest, and empties into the Gǔ River,
where there is plenty of mí stone
and lú cinnabar.
Another fifty li to the west,
there is Gǔshān,
on which there is much paper mulberry,
and below it much mulberry.
Shuǎng Shuǐ emerges from here,
and flows northwest into Gǔ Shuǐ,
in which there is much green jade.
Another seventy-two li to the west,
there is Mount Mì,
with much jade on its southern side,
and much iron on its northern side.
The Háo River originates here,
flowing southward into the Luò River,
where many spiral tortoises are found.
They have the appearance of a bird's head and a turtle's tail,
and their sound is like splitting wood.
There is no grass or trees.
Another hundred li to the west,
there is a mountain called Chángshí,
devoid of grass and trees,
but rich in metal and jade.
To its west lies a valley,
named Gòng Valley,
abundant with bamboo.
The Gòng River originates here,
flowing southwest into the Luò River,
and within it are many resonant stones.
Another one hundred forty miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Fù Shān,
with no grass or trees,
but abundant in yao and bi jade.
The Yānrǎn River originates from its southern side,
flows southward, and empties into the Luò River,
where there are many human-fish.
To its west lies a forest,
named Fán Zhǒng.
The Gǔ River emerges from there,
runs eastward, and pours into the Luò River,
containing plenty of yān jade.
Another fifty li to the west,
there is Mount Tuó,
where the trees are mostly ailanthus,
and there are many bèi trees.
On its southern side, there is much metal and jade,
on its northern side, there is much iron,
and many artemisia plants.
The Tuó River flows from here,
running northward to empty into the Yellow River.
In it, there are many xiūpì fish,
which look like frogs but have white beaks,
and their call resembles that of an owl.
Eating them can cure white ringworm.
Another ninety li to the west,
there is a mountain called Chángzhēng Zhī Shān,
devoid of grass and trees,
with much chalk.
The Qiáo Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing northeast into the Hé,
and within it, there is much dark green jade.
The Zī Shuǐ also originates from here,
flowing north into the Hé.
Another ninety li to the west,
there is Mount Kuāfù.
Its trees are mostly palms and nanmu,
and there are many bamboo arrows.
Among its beasts are many zuò cattle
and qián sheep,
while its birds are mostly bì pheasants.
On its southern side, there is much jade,
and on its northern side, much iron.
To the north, there is a forest,
named the Peach Forest,
which spans three hundred li in circumference,
and within it are many horses.
The lake water flows out from here,
running northward to empty into the River,
and in it, there is much yān jade.
Another ninety li to the west,
there is Yánghuà Mountain.
Its southern side is rich in metal and jade,
while its northern side abounds in realgar and orpiment.
Among its grasses, many are yams,
and many are bitter and pungent.
Their shape resembles that of the catalpa tree,
their fruit is like a melon,
their taste is sour and sweet,
and eating them cures malaria.
Yángshuǐ originates here,
flowing southwest into the Luò River,
and within it, there are many human-faced fish.
Ménshuǐ originates here,
flowing northeast into the Hé River,
and within it, there are many black flints.
Gūzhīshuǐ emerges from its northern side,
flowing east into Ménshuǐ,
and on its banks, there is much copper.
From Ménshuǐ to the Hé River,
it is seven hundred and ninety li before entering the Luòshuǐ.
The head of the Gǎodī Mountains,
from the Píngféng Mountain to the Yánghuá Mountain,
comprises a total of fourteen mountains,
spanning seven hundred and ninety li.
The sacred mountain lies within them,
and it is worshipped in the sixth month,
following the sacrificial rites of the other sacred mountains,
to bring peace and stability to the world.
The first mountain of the Kǔ Shān range in the Central Seventh Classic,
is called Xiūyǔ Zhī Shān.
On its summit, there are stones,
named Dìtái Zhī Qí,
which are of five colors and patterned,
their shape resembling quail eggs.
The stones of Dìtái
are used to pray to the hundred deities,
and wearing them prevents bewitchment.
There is a grass there,
its appearance like yarrow,
with red leaves and clustered roots,
named Fēngtiáo,
which can be used to make arrow shafts.
Three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Gǔzhōng,
where the Divine Terrace is used to feast the hundred spirits.
There is a plant there,
with a square stem and yellow flowers,
round leaves arranged in three layers,
named Yānsuān,
which can be used to counteract poison.
On its upper parts, there is an abundance of coarse whetstones,
and on its lower parts, fine whetstones.
Two hundred li further east,
there is Mount Gūyáo,
where the daughter of an emperor died.
Her name was Nǚshī,
and she transformed into a yáo plant.
Its leaves grow in clusters,
its flowers are yellow,
and its fruit resembles that of the rabbit-foot clover.
If one consumes it, they will become charming to others.
Another twenty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Kǔ Shān.
There is a beast here,
named Shān Gāo,
whose form resembles a chase,
as red as cinnabar fire,
and skilled in cursing.
On its summit, there is a tree,
named Huáng Jí,
with yellow flowers and round leaves,
its fruit resembling an orchid,
and consuming it causes infertility.
There is an herb here,
with round leaves and no stem,
bearing red flowers but no fruit,
named Wú Tiáo,
and taking it prevents goiters.
Twenty-seven li further east,
there is Mount Dǔ,
where the deity Tiānyú dwells,
and there are many strange winds and rains.
On its summit grows a tree,
named Tiānpián,
with a square stem and a sunflower-like appearance,
and eating it prevents choking.
Another fifty-two li to the east,
there is Mount Fànggāo.
The Míng River flows out from here,
running southward into the Yī River,
and in it, there is an abundance of dark green jade.
There is a tree here,
its leaves resembling those of the locust tree,
with yellow flowers but bearing no fruit,
its name is Méngmù,
and wearing it dispels confusion.
There is a beast here,
its form like that of a bee,
with a forked tail and a reversed tongue,
skilled at calling out,
its name is Wénwén.
Another fifty-seven li to the east,
there is Mount Dàkǔ,
rich in Tūfú jade,
and abundant in elk jade.
There is a plant here,
whose leaves resemble those of the elm,
with a square stem and blue markings,
named Niúshāng.
Its roots have blue patterns,
and those who consume it will not suffer from fainting spells,
and it can ward off weapons.
The Mad Water emerges from its southern side,
flowing southwest into the Yi River,
where many three-legged turtles are found.
Eating them prevents major illnesses,
and it can cure swellings.
Another seventy li to the east,
there is Mount Bànshí.
On its summit grows an herb,
which sprouts and flourishes,
reaching a height of over ten feet.
It has red leaves and red blossoms,
blooming but bearing no fruit.
Its name is Jiāróng,
and those who consume it fear not thunder.
The Láixū River flows from its southern side,
running westward into the Yī River.
In its waters dwell many lún fish,
marked with black patterns,
resembling crucian carp in appearance.
Those who eat them will not feel sleepy.
The Hé River emerges from its northern side,
flowing northward into the Luò River.
It abounds with téng fish,
shaped like mandarin fish,
dwelling in the thoroughfares,
with blue patterns and red tails.
Those who consume them will not develop abscesses,
and it can be used to treat goiters.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is Mount Shǎoshì,
where a hundred plants and trees grow in clusters.
On its summit, there is a tree,
named Dìxiū,
with leaves shaped like those of a poplar,
its branches spreading in five directions,
bearing yellow flowers and black fruits.
Those who eat it will not feel anger.
On its heights, there is much jade,
and at its foot, much iron.
The Xiū River flows from it,
running northward into the Luò River,
in which there are many Tí fish,
shaped like the Zhōuwèi monkey but with long spurs,
white feet that face each other.
Those who eat them will not suffer from gu diseases,
and it can ward off weapons.
Another thirty li to the east,
stands Mount Tàishì.
Upon it grows a tree,
with leaves shaped like lamb's quarters but with red veins,
named Yǒumù.
Those who wear it will not feel jealousy.
There is also an herb,
shaped like a plant,
with white flowers and black fruits,
glossy like wild grapes,
named Yáocǎo.
Those who wear it will not be troubled by nightmares,
and the mountain is rich in beautiful stones.
Another thirty li to the north,
there is a mountain called Jiǎng Shān,
on which there is much jade,
abundant wild mulberry trees,
and numerous cypress trees.
Among the trees there,
there is one named Dì Wū,
whose leaves resemble those of the pepper plant,
with thorns turned inward and red fruits,
capable of warding off evil.
Another thirty li to the north,
there is Mount Yīngliáng,
on which there is much dark green jade,
resting upon black stones.
Another thirty li to the east,
there is Fúxì Mountain.
There is a tree there,
with leaves like the tree of heaven and red fruit,
named Kàngmù;
eating it prevents possession.
The Sìshuǐ River originates here,
flowing north to empty into the Yellow River.
To its east there is a valley,
thus named Shégǔ (Snake Valley),
on which grows much xìxīn (Asarum).
Another forty li to the east,
there is Mount Shàoxíng.
There is a plant here,
named Gāng Cǎo,
with leaves shaped like those of the sunflower,
but with red stems and white flowers.
Its fruit resembles that of the wild grape,
and eating it makes one free from foolishness.
The Qìnán River originates here,
and flows northward into the Mò River.
Another ten lǐ to the southeast,
there is Mount Tài.
There is a plant there,
called lí,
whose leaves resemble qiū but have red flowers,
and can be used to cure abscesses.
The Tài River originates from its southern side,
and flows southeast into the Mò River,
while the Chéng River originates from its northern side,
and flows northeast into the Mò.
Twenty li further to the east,
there is Mò Shān,
abundant with red gold on its summit.
Mò Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing northward and emptying into Mò.
Another twenty-five li to the east,
there is Yì Shān,
on which there is much white metal,
and much iron.
Yì Shuǐ flows from here,
running north and emptying into the Hé.
Another thirty-five li to the east,
there is Mǐn Shān.
On its summit grows a tree,
whose form resembles that of the chaste tree,
with white blossoms and red fruits,
named Jì Bǎi.
Those who consume it do not feel cold.
On its sunny side, there is much Tú Fú jade.
Another thirty li to the east,
stands Mount Dàguī,
on its shady side, there is abundant iron,
fine jade,
and green chalk.
There is a plant here,
shaped like yarrow but hairy,
with blue flowers and white fruit,
named hěn;
consuming it prevents premature death,
and it can cure abdominal illnesses.
Of the first range of the Kǔ Mountains,
from the Xiūyǔ Mountains to the Dàguī Mountains,
there are altogether nineteen mountains,
spanning one thousand one hundred and eighty-four lǐ.
Among the sixteen deities,
all have the bodies of pigs and human faces.
For their sacrifices:
a whole sheep is offered as a ritual animal,
and an ornamental jade is buried as an offering.
The Kǔ Mountains,
Shǎoshì,
and Tàishì are all ancestral peaks,
and for their sacrifices:
the offerings include the set of the Great Sacrifice,
with auspicious jade used as ornaments.
The forms of these deities all have human faces and three heads,
while the rest of the associated deities have pig bodies and human faces.
The first mountain of the Jīngshān range in the Central Eighth Classic,
is called Jǐngshān.
On its summit, there is an abundance of metals and jade,
and its trees are mostly oak and sandalwood.
The Jūshuǐ River originates from here,
flowing southeast into the Yangtze River.
In its waters, there are many red granules,
and numerous patterned fish.
A hundred li to the northeast,
there is Mount Jīng,
on its northern side there is much iron,
on its southern side there is much red gold,
within it there are many yaks,
many leopards and tigers,
its trees are mostly pines and cypresses,
its grasses are mostly bamboos,
and many oranges and pomelos.
The Zhāng River flows out from here,
and runs southeast into the Suī,
within it there is much yellow gold,
and many shark fish.
Its beasts are mostly wild boars and large deer.
Another one hundred fifty li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Jiāo Shān,
on which there is much jade,
and below it much green mineral pigment,
its trees being mostly pines and cypresses,
with many peach-branch bamboos and hook-tip bamboos.
The spirit Tuó Wéi dwells there,
whose form is like a human face,
with ram's horns and tiger's claws,
constantly roaming in the abyss of the Jū and Zhāng rivers,
emitting light upon entering and exiting.
Another hundred and twenty li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Nǚjī Zhī Shān.
On its summit, there is much jade,
and at its base, abundant gold.
Among the beasts, there are many leopards and tigers,
numerous wild donkeys and elk,
as well as muntjacs and river deer.
The birds are mostly white pheasants,
many long-tailed pheasants,
and numerous poisonous Zhen birds.
Another two hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Yízhūzhī Shān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
and at its foot, an abundance of green mineral pigment.
The Wéi Shuǐ originates here,
flowing southward into the Zhāng,
and within it, there is much white jade.
Another three hundred fifty li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Lún Shān.
Its trees are largely catalpa and nanmu,
with abundant peach-bamboo,
and plenty of hawthorn, chestnut, orange, and pomelo trees.
Its beasts are mostly black-haired female deer, elk-like creatures,
antelopes,
and swift-running beasts.
Another two hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Lùguī Zhī Shān,
on which there is much Túfú jade,
below it there is much white clay,
and its trees are mostly the niǔ and jiāng kinds.
Another hundred and thirty miles to the east,
there is a mountain called Guāng Shān,
on its summit there is much jade,
and at its base, abundant water.
The deity Jì Méng dwells there,
whose form is a human body with a dragon's head.
He constantly roams in the Zhāng Abyss,
and whenever he enters or exits, there are sure to be whirlwinds and torrential rains.
Another one hundred fifty li to the east,
there is Qí Shān.
On its southern side, there is much red metal,
and on its northern side, much white jade-like stone.
On its summit, there is abundant gold and jade,
while at its base, there is plentiful green mineral pigment.
Among its trees, the Ailanthus is most common.
The spirit Shè Tuó dwells there,
whose form is that of a human body with a square face and three feet.
Another hundred and thirty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Tóngshān,
on which there is much gold, silver, and iron.
Its trees are mostly paper mulberry, oak, hawthorn, chestnut, tangerine, and pomelo,
and its beasts are mostly bào.
Further northeast one hundred li,
there is a mountain called Měi Shān.
Its beasts are mostly rhinoceroses and cattle,
many wild boars and elk,
numerous pigs and deer.
On its upper parts, there is much metal,
and below it, much green mineral pigment.
Another hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Dàyáo Zhī Shān.
Its trees are mostly pines and cypresses,
with many catalpas and mulberries,
and numerous oaks.
Its grasses are mostly bamboos,
and its beasts are mostly leopards, tigers, antelopes, and tapirs.
Three hundred li further to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Líng Shān,
on which there is much metal and jade,
beneath which there is much green indigo,
and whose trees are mostly peach, plum, apricot, and almond.
Another seventy li to the northeast,
there is Lóngshān,
on which there are many parasitic trees,
and on its upper parts, much green jade,
while below, there is abundant red tin,
and among the grasses, many Táozhī and Gōuduān bamboos.
Another fifty li to the southeast,
stands Héngshān,
its summit rich with parasitic trees, paper mulberries, and oaks,
abundant in yellow chalk and white chalk.
Another seventy li to the southeast,
there is Stone Mountain,
on which there is much metal,
and below it much green mineral pigment,
with many parasitic trees.
Another hundred and twenty li to the south,
there is Ruò Shān,
on which there is much Tūfú jade,
much red ochre,
much Guī stone,
many parasitic trees,
and many three-bristle cudrania.
Another one hundred and twenty li to the southeast,
there is Zhìshān,
abundant in beautiful stones,
and plentiful in mulberry trees.
Another one hundred fifty li to the southeast,
there is Yù Shān,
on its summit much gold and jade,
at its base much green jade and iron,
and among its trees many cypresses.
Another seventy li to the southeast,
there is Huān Shān,
where the trees are mostly sandalwood,
abundant in Guī stones,
and rich in white tin.
Yù Shuǐ emerges from its summit,
and submerges beneath it,
with many whetstones within its waters.
Another one hundred and fifty li to the northeast,
there is Mount Rénjǔ,
where the trees are mostly paper mulberry and oak,
its southern side is rich in red gold,
and its northern side has abundant red ochre.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is Shīměi Mountain.
On its sunny side, there is much whetstone,
and on its shady side, much green mineral pigment.
Among the trees, there are many cypresses,
many sandalwoods,
many three-bristle cudranias,
and among the grasses, many bamboos.
Another two hundred li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Qíngǔ,
where the trees are mostly paper mulberry, oak, pepper trees, and three-bristle cudrania,
on its upper parts there is much white jade-like stone,
at its foot much scrubbing stone,
among its beasts many boars and deer,
many white rhinoceroses,
and among its birds many zhen birds.
Of the Jīngshān range,
from Jǐngshān Mountain to Qíngǔ Mountain,
there are altogether twenty-three mountains,
spanning two thousand eight hundred and ninety li.
The spirits here all have bird bodies and human faces.
For their sacrifices:
use one rooster for prayer and burial,
use one patterned jade tablet,
and offer polished rice as sacrificial grain.
Jiāoshān Mountain
is the ancestral mountain,
and its sacrifices:
use fine wine and a young animal for prayer and burial,
with a jade disc adorned with animal fur.
The first mountain of the Mínshān range in the Central Ninth Classic,
is called the Nǚjī Mountains.
On its summit, there is an abundance of graphite,
its trees are mostly spindle trees and oaks,
and its grasses are largely chrysanthemums and artemisia.
The Luò River originates here,
flowing eastward into the Yangtze River,
within which there is much realgar,
and its wild beasts are mostly tigers and leopards.
Further northeast three hundred li,
is Mount Mín,
the Jiāng River originates from there,
flowing northeast into the sea,
in which there are many fine turtles,
and many tuó (Chinese alligators).
On its heights there is much metal and jade,
at its base there is much white mǐn (a stone resembling jade),
its trees are mostly plum and pear,
its beasts are mostly rhinoceroses and elephants,
many kuí oxen (a legendary large ox),
its birds are mostly hàn and bì (types of pheasants).
Further northeast one hundred and forty li,
there is a mountain called Láishān,
from which the Jiāngshuǐ River flows,
running eastward and emptying into the Great River.
On its southern side, there is much gold,
on its northern side, many elk and deer,
among its trees, many sandalwood and mulberry,
among its grasses, many shallots and chives,
abundant medicinal herbs,
and kōngduó plants.
Another one hundred fifty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Jūshān.
The Jiāngshuǐ River originates from it,
flowing eastward into the Dàjiāng River.
In it, there are many strange snakes,
and many zhì fish.
Among its trees are many oak and nǐu trees,
and many plum and catalpa trees.
Its beasts include many kuíniú, líng, chuò, xī, and sì.
There is a bird there;
it looks like an owl with a red body and a white head,
its name is Qièzhī,
and it can be used to ward off fire.
Another three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Gāoliáng Zhī Shān,
on which there is much chalk,
and at its foot, many whetstones.
Its trees are mostly peach-branch bamboos and hook-tip bamboos.
There is a plant here,
shaped like a sunflower but with red flowers,
bearing pod-like fruits,
and white calyxes,
which can be used to make horses run swiftly.
Another four hundred li to the east,
there is Shé Shān.
On its summit, there is much gold,
and at its base, much white clay.
Among its trees are many xún
and yùzhāng.
Its plants are mostly jiāróng
and shǎoxīn.
There is a beast here
that looks like a fox
but has a white tail and long ears,
named shíláng.
When it appears, there will be military conflicts within the state.
Five hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Gé Shān.
On its southern side, there is much metal,
and on its northern side, much white jade-like stone.
The Pú Hōng River flows from here,
running eastward and emptying into the river,
in which there is much white jade.
Among the beasts, there are many rhinoceroses, elephants, bears, and brown bears,
and many apes and long-tailed monkeys.
Three hundred li further to the northeast,
stands Mount Yúyáng,
abundant with metal and jade on its summit,
and rich in green minerals below,
its trees mostly catalpa and mulberry,
its grasses largely violet.
The Xú River flows from here,
running eastward into the Yangtze,
its waters teeming with cinnabar granules.
Another two hundred fifty li to the east,
there is Qí Shān,
on its summit much white metal is found,
and at its base much iron,
its trees are mostly plum and catalpa,
and there are many kinds of thorny trees and oaks.
Jiǎn Shuǐ emerges from here,
flowing southeast to pour into the Jiāng.
Three hundred li further east,
stands Mount Gōuní,
with abundant jade on its summit,
plentiful gold at its base,
trees dominated by oaks and mulberries,
and vegetation rich in peonies.
Another one hundred fifty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Fēngyǔ,
on which there is much white metal,
and below it much graphite,
among its trees many Zōu and Shàn,
and many poplars.
The Xuānyú River flows out from here,
running eastward and emptying into the river,
in which there are many snakes.
Among its beasts are many wild donkeys and elk,
many Zhǔ, leopards, and tigers,
and among its birds many white pheasants.
Another two hundred li to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Yù Shān.
On its southern side, there is an abundance of copper,
and on its northern side, much red gold.
The trees there are mostly camphor, nanmu, oak, and hackberry,
the beasts mostly boars, deer, antelopes, and tapirs,
and the birds mostly poisonous pheasants.
Another one hundred fifty miles to the east,
is called Xióng Shān.
There is a cave there,
the cave of bears,
from which divine beings often emerge.
It opens in summer and closes in winter;
this cave,
if it opens in winter, then there will surely be warfare.
On its summit, there is much white jade,
at its base, much white gold,
its trees are mostly chū and willow,
its grasses mostly kòu tuō.
Another one hundred and forty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Guīshān,
with many beautiful jades and red gold on its southern side,
and much iron on its northern side.
The trees there are mostly peach branches, brambles, and millet.
Another two hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Gé Shān,
on which there is much red gold,
and below it, much jiān stone.
Its trees are mostly pear, chestnut, orange, pomelo, oak, and catalpa,
its beasts mostly antelopes and zhuó,
and its grasses mostly jiā róng.
Further east one hundred seventy li,
there is a mountain called Jiǎchāo,
on its sunny side there is much yellow chalk,
on its shady side there is much beautiful red ochre,
among its trees are many crabapples, chestnuts, tangerines, and pomelos,
and among its plants there is much dragon's beard grass.
The Min Mountain range begins,
from the Nǚjī Mountain to the Jiǎchāo Mountains,
totaling sixteen mountains,
spanning three thousand five hundred li.
Their deities all have horse bodies and dragon heads.
The sacrifices for them:
use a rooster buried as the fur offering,
and polished rice as the sacrificial grain.
The Wén Mountain,
Gōunì,
Fēngyǔ,
and Guī Mountains,
are all burial mounds.
The sacrifices for them:
offer wine,
provide a shǎoláo sacrifice,
and adorn with a single auspicious jade.
The Xióng Mountain,
is an imperial mountain,
its sacrifice:
offer wine,
provide a tàiláo sacrifice,
and adorn with a single bi disc.
Perform the shield dance,
to use arms for exorcism;
for prayers, perform the dance with jade pendants and ceremonial caps.
The first mountain of the Middle Tenth Classic,
is called Shǒuyáng Mountain,
on which there is much metal and jade,
but no grasses or trees.
Another fifty miles to the west,
there is a mountain called Hǔwěi,
where trees are abundant with pepper and Jǔ trees,
and there is plenty of feng stone.
On its sunny side, there is much red gold,
and on its shady side, there is much iron.
Another fifty li to the southwest,
there is Mount Fánkuì,
where the trees are mostly oak and spindle trees,
and the grasses are mostly branched and curved.
Another twenty li to the southwest,
there is Mount Yǒngshí,
devoid of grass and trees,
abundant in white metal,
and with plentiful water.
Another twenty li to the west,
there is Mount Fùzhōu,
where the trees are mostly sandalwood,
and on its sunny side, there is abundant gold.
There is a bird here,
whose shape resembles an owl,
but with one foot and a pig's tail,
its name is Qǐzhǒng,
and when it appears, the state will suffer a great plague.
Another thirty li to the west,
there is Chǔ Shān,
abounding in parasitic trees,
abundant with pepper trees and Jǔ trees,
rich in three-bristle cudrania,
and plentiful in white clay.
Another twenty li to the west,
there is Mount Yòuyuán,
where the sunny side abounds with green mineral pigments,
the shady side is rich in iron,
and among the birds, mynas are plentiful.
Another fifty miles to the west,
there is Zhuōshān,
where the trees are mostly paper mulberry, oak, and Chinese hackberry,
and on its sunny side, there is much jade of the Túfú kind.
Another seventy li to the west,
there is Mount Bǐng,
where the trees are mostly catalpa and sandalwood,
and there are many long-shafted axes.
Of the range of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
from Shǒu Mountain to Bǐng Mountain,
there are altogether nine mountains,
spanning two hundred and sixty-seven li.
The spirits here all have dragon bodies and human faces.
For their sacrifices:
the sacrificial animal is a rooster buried in the earth,
and the offerings consist of five types of grains.
Dǔ Mountain,
is a tomb mound,
for its sacrifice:
a shǎoláo offering is prepared,
with wine presented in the ritual,
and a jade disc buried along with the sacrificial animal.
Guī Mountain,
is an imperial mountain,
for its sacrifice, wine is presented,
and a tàiláo offering is prepared;
together with two shamans and invokers performing a dance,
and a jade disc offered.
The first mountain of the Jīng Shān range in the "Middle Eleven Mountains Classic"
is called Yìwàng Zhī Shān.
Tuān Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Jì River.
Kuàng Shuǐ also originates from here,
flowing southeast into the Hàn River,
where there are many jiāo (aquatic dragons).
On its upper slopes, there are many pine and cypress trees,
while at its base, there is an abundance of lacquer and catalpa trees.
Its southern side is rich in red gold,
and its northern side has much mǐn (a jade-like stone).
Further northeast one hundred fifty miles,
lies Cháogē Mountain.
The Wǔ River flows out from here,
running southeast into the Róng,
in which there are many human-fish.
On its heights grow many catalpas and nanmu trees,
and among its beasts are many antelopes and elk.
There is a plant here,
named Mǎng Cǎo,
which can be used to poison fish.
Another two hundred li to the southeast,
there is Mount Dìqūn.
On its sunny side, there is much Tūfú jade,
and on its shady side, much iron.
The Dìqūn River emerges from its summit
and flows underground beneath it,
where there are many singing snakes.
Another fifty li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Shì Shān,
on which there is an abundance of leeks.
There is a well there,
named Tiān Jǐng,
which has water in summer
but dries up in winter.
On the mountain, there are many mulberry trees,
as well as abundant fine chalk,
gold, and jade.
Another two hundred li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Qiánshān,
where the trees are mostly oaks,
and many cypresses,
with abundant metal on its southern side,
and much red ochre on its northern side.
Three hundred li further to the southeast,
stands Mount Fēng.
There is a beast here,
shaped like an ape,
with red eyes,
a red beak,
and a yellow body,
named Yōng Hé.
Its appearance foretells great terror in the state.
The deity Gēng Fù dwells there,
often roaming in the clear, cold abyss,
emitting light upon entering and exiting,
and his sighting leads to the state's downfall.
There are nine bells here,
known to chime at frost.
Its summit is rich in metal,
and below, there is an abundance of paper mulberry, oak, Chinese hackberry, and oak trees.
Another eight hundred lǐ to the northeast,
there is a mountain called Tùchuáng.
On its southern side, there is much iron,
and among its trees, many are shǔyù,
while among its grasses, many are jīgǔ.
Their roots are like chicken eggs,
their flavor is sour and sweet,
and eating them is beneficial to people.
Another sixty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Pí Shān,
abundant in chalk,
rich in red ochre,
with trees mostly of pine and cypress.
Another sixty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Yáobì,
where the trees are mostly catalpa and nanmu,
on its shady side there is much azurite,
and on its sunny side, much white metal.
There is a bird here,
whose form is like a pheasant,
that constantly eats insects,
named Zhèn.
Forty li further east,
stands Mount Gōnglí,
from which the Yù River flows,
running southward into the Hàn River.
There is a bird here,
named Yīngsháo,
resembling a magpie in appearance,
with red eyes,
a red beak,
a white body,
and a tail shaped like a ladle,
whose call echoes its own name.
There are many zuò oxen
and numerous qián sheep.
Further northeast for fifty li,
there is a mountain called Zhìzhú Zhī Shān,
on which grow many pines, cypresses, catalpas, and oaks.
Another hundred li to the northwest,
there is a mountain called Jǐnlǐzhīshān.
On its summit, there are many pine and cypress trees,
and fine catalpas.
On its shady side, there is abundant cinnabar and ochre,
and much gold.
Among its beasts, there are many leopards and tigers.
There is a bird here,
whose shape resembles a magpie,
with a green body and a white beak,
white eyes and a white tail,
named Qīnggēng.
It can be used to ward off epidemics,
and its call is its own name.
Another thirty li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Yīgū Zhī Shān,
on which there are many niǔ and jiāng trees,
and much jū.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a dog,
with tiger claws and armor,
its name is Lín,
skilled at Yǎngbì,
and those who eat it will not suffer from wind ailments.
Another thirty-five li to the southeast,
there is Jígǔ Mountain,
abundant in fine jade,
many black leopards,
numerous wild donkeys and elk,
and plenty of antelopes and a type of deer-like animal.
Its southern side is rich in stone resembling jade,
while its northern side has much azurite and malachite.
Another forty li to the southeast,
there is Jī Shān,
on which there are many beautiful catalpa trees,
many mulberry trees,
and among the grasses, many chives.
Another fifty li to the southeast,
there is Mount Gāoqián.
Upon it, there is water,
very cold and clear,
the brew of the Divine Terrace,
and those who drink it do not suffer from heart pain.
On its summit, there is gold,
and at its base, there is red ochre.
Another thirty li to the southeast,
is called Yóuxìzhī Shān,
abundant with niǔ, jiāng, and gǔ trees,
rich in jade,
and plentiful in fēngshí.
Another thirty-five li to the southeast,
there is Cóng Mountain,
on which there are many pine and cypress trees,
and beneath it, abundant bamboo.
The Cóng River originates from its summit,
and flows hidden beneath it,
in which there are many three-legged turtles,
with forked tails,
and eating them prevents gu diseases.
Another thirty li to the southeast,
there is Mount Yīngzhēn,
with many pines and cypresses on its summit,
and numerous catalpas and cedrelas at its base.
Another thirty li to the southeast,
there is Mount Bì.
The waters of the Imperial Garden originate here,
flowing northeast and pouring into the Shì River,
in which there is much crystal,
many flood dragons,
and on its summit, abundant Túfú jade.
Another twenty li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Lèmǎ.
There is a beast there,
whose form resembles a hedgehog,
and is as red as cinnabar fire.
Its name is Lì,
and when it appears, the state will suffer a great plague.
Another twenty-five li to the southeast,
is called Zhēn Shān,
from which the Shì Shuǐ originates,
flowing southeast and joining the Rǔ Shuǐ,
in which there are many human-fish,
many flood dragons,
and many jié.
Another forty li to the east,
there is Yīng Shān,
at its foot there is much green ochre,
and on its summit, much metal and jade.
Another thirty li to the east,
there is Mount Hǔshǒu,
abundant with hemp, oak, and scrubby trees.
Twenty li further east,
there is Mount Yīnghóu,
on its summit there is much sealing stone,
and at its base much red tin.
Fifty li further east,
there is Mount Dàshú.
The Shā River flows out from here,
running northeast and pouring into the Shì River,
where there is an abundance of white clay.
Another forty li to the east,
there is Bēi Shān,
on which there are many peach, plum, wild ginger, and catalpa trees,
and many vines.
Another thirty li to the east,
stands Yǐdìzhīshān,
on its summit abundant with jade,
and at its foot rich with gold.
There is a beast there,
shaped like a Fei rat,
with white ears and a white snout,
named Jūrú,
whose appearance foretells great military strife in the state.
Another thirty li to the east,
there is Ní Shān,
from which the Ní Shuǐ originates above,
and disappears underground below,
with an abundance of fine chalk within it.
On its summit, there is much gold,
and at its base, much qīnghù.
Another thirty li to the east,
there is Yǎ Shān.
The Lǐ Shuǐ originates from here,
flowing eastward into the Shì Shuǐ,
where there are many large fish.
On its heights, there are many fine mulberry trees,
and at its base, much hemp grows,
as well as abundant red gold.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is Xuān Shān.
Lún Shuǐ originates here,
flowing southeast into Shì Shuǐ,
and within it are many jiāo.
Upon the mountain grows a mulberry tree,
fifty chi in girth,
its branches extending in all directions,
its leaves over a chi in size,
with red veins, yellow flowers, and green calyxes,
named Dìnǚzhīsāng.
Another forty-five li to the east,
there is Mount Héng,
on which there is much green ore,
many mulberry trees,
and among its birds, many mynahs.
Forty li further to the east,
there is Fēng Shān.
Its summit abounds with féngshí,
its trees are mostly mulberry,
and there are many yángtáo trees.
They resemble peach trees but have square stems,
and can be used to treat skin ailments.
Another seventy li to the east,
there is a mountain called Yù Shān,
on which there is much beautiful jade,
and below it, much gold.
Among its grasses, many are Jīgǔ.
Thirty li further east,
there is a mountain called Xiān Shān.
Its trees are mostly oak, Chinese hackberry, and thorny limeberry trees;
its grasses are mostly winter-growing plants.
On its southern side, there is much gold,
and on its northern side, much iron.
There is a beast here,
whose shape resembles a hairless dog,
with a red beak,
red eyes,
and a white tail.
When it appears, there will be fire in the city;
its name is Yíjí.
Another thirty li to the east,
is called Gāo Shān,
its southern side is rich in metal,
its northern side is rich in beautiful stones.
Gāo Shuǐ originates from here,
flows eastward and pours into Lǐ Shuǐ,
within which there are many brittle stones.
Another twenty-five li to the east,
there is the Dàzhī Mountain,
with much metal on its southern side,
and its trees are mostly paper mulberries and oaks,
with no grass.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is the Qūwú Mountain,
where the trees are mostly oak.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Shēng Xiōng,
where the trees are mostly paper mulberry,
and there is much jade.
On its summit, there is an abundance of sealing stones.
Another fifty li to the east,
there is Mount Dàguī,
on its sunny side, there is much red gold,
on its shady side, there are many whetstones.
Another ten li to the east,
there is a mountain called Zhǒngjiù,
devoid of grass and trees.
Further northeast seventy li,
there is Mount Lìshí,
where the trees are mostly brambles and paper mulberries,
its southern side rich in gold,
and its northern side abundant in whetstones.
There is a beast here,
whose form resembles a wildcat,
with a white head and tiger-like claws,
named Liángqú.
When it appears, the state will face great military conflicts.
Another one hundred and twenty li to the southeast,
there is a mountain called Qiú Shān.
The Qiú River originates from its summit,
and flows underground at its base,
where fine red ochre is found.
Among its trees are many oaks,
and abundant bamboos.
On its sunny side, there is much gold,
and on its shady side, much iron.
Another two hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Chǒuyángzhīshān,
on which there are many chou and ju trees.
There is a bird here,
whose appearance is like a crow but with red feet,
named Zhìtú,
that can be used to ward off fire.
Another three hundred li to the east,
there is a mountain called Ào Shān,
on which there are many cypress, nǐu, and jiāng trees,
and on its sunny side, much jade of the tūfú kind.
Ào Shuǐ flows out from here,
and runs eastward into Shì Shuǐ.
Another thirty-five li to the east,
there is Mount Fú,
where the trees are mostly oak,
on its summit there is much sealing stone,
and at its base, abundant red tin.
Three hundred li further east,
there is a mountain called Yǎoshān,
on which there is an abundance of fine rong grass,
and much metal and jade.
Another three hundred fifty li to the east,
there is a mountain called Jī Shān,
where the trees are mostly oak, sandalwood, and Chinese hackberry,
and the grasses are mostly fragrant.
There is a beast here,
shaped like a pig,
with a yellow body,
a white head,
and a white tail,
named Wén Lín,
whose appearance causes great winds throughout the world.
Of the range of Jīngshān mountains,
from Yìwàng Mountain to Jǐ Mountain,
there are forty-eight mountains in total,
spanning three thousand seven hundred and thirty-two li.
The spirits all have the bodies of pigs and human heads.
The sacrifices for them:
use one rooster for the fur-offering prayer,
bury one jade tablet,

There are nine hills,
bound by water:
named the Hill of Táotáng,
the Hill of Shūdé,
the Hill of Mèngyíng,
the Hill of Kūnwú,
the Hill of Hēibái,
the Hill of Chìwàng,
the Hill of Cānwèi,
the Hill of Wǔfū,
and the Hill of Shénmín.
There is a tree,
with green leaves and purple stems,
dark flowers and yellow fruit,
named Jiànmù.
It stands a hundred ren high without branches,
above it has nine curved limbs,
below it has nine twisted roots,
its fruit resembles hemp,
its leaves are like awn grass,
where Dàhào once passed,
and which Huángdì fashioned.
There is the Yàyǔ,
with a dragon's head,
that eats people.
There is a beast,
with a human face,
named Xīngxing.
In the southwest there was the State of Bā.
Dà Hào gave birth to Xián Niǎo,
Xián Niǎo gave birth to Chéng Lí,
Chéng Lí gave birth to Hòu Zhào,
Hòu Zhào was the one who first became the Bā people.
There is a state called Liúhuáng Xīnshì,
its territory spans three hundred li square,
and what emerges from it is dust.
There is Mount Bāsuì,
from which the Miǎnshuǐ River flows.
There is also the land of Zhuǎnjuǎn.
There are black snakes,
with green heads,
that devour elephants.
In the south, there are Gàn giants,
with human faces and long arms,
black bodies covered in hair,
and reversed heels.
They laugh when they see people laugh,
and their lips cover their faces,
which is why they flee immediately.
There were also black-skinned people,
with tiger heads and bird feet,
holding snakes in both hands,
just then eating them.
There are the Yíng people,
who have bird-like feet.
There is a giant pig.
There is a people called the Miáo.
There is a deity among them,
with a human head and a serpent body,
as long as a carriage shaft,
having heads on both sides,
clad in purple robes,
and wearing a felt cap,
named Yánwéi.
If a ruler can capture and offer sacrifices to it,
they will become the overlord of the world.
The luánniǎo sings of its own accord,
the fèngniǎo dances of its own accord.
The fèngniǎo's head bears the character for virtue,
its wings bear the character for compliance,
its breast bears the character for benevolence,
its back bears the character for righteousness,
and when it appears, all under heaven is in harmony.
There is also a blue beast like a rabbit,
named the Jūnjū dog.
There are kingfishers.
There are peacocks.
Within the South Sea, there is Héngshān.
There is Jūnshān.
There is Guìshān.
There is a mountain named the Capital of Sāntiānzǐ.
In the south, there lies the Cāngwú Hills,
the Cāngwú Abyss,
within which stands the Jiǔyí Mountains,
where Shùn was buried,
located within the boundaries of Chángshā Línglíng.
Within the North Sea,
there is a mountain called Shéshān,
from which the Shéshuǐ River originates,
flowing eastward into the sea.
There are birds of five colors,
whose flight can obscure an entire region,
named Yìniǎo.
There is also the Bùjù Mountain,
where Qiǎochuí is buried to its west.
Within the North Sea,
there is an assistant bound backward with thief's fetters,
carrying a spear and often turning his back,
named Xiānggù's Corpse.
Bóyífù gave birth to Xīyuè,
Xīyuè gave birth to Xiānlóng,
Xiānlóng was the first to father the Díqiāng,
the Díqiāng bear the surname Qǐ.
Within the Northern Sea,
there is a mountain,
named Yōudū zhī Shān,
from which the Black Water flows.
Upon it are black birds,
black snakes,
black leopards,
black tigers,
and black foxes with bushy tails.
There is the Dà Xuán zhī Shān.
There are the people of the Xuán Qiū.
There is the Dà Yōu zhī Guó.
There are the people with red shins.
There is the land of Dīnglíng,
whose people have hair from the knees down,
and horse hooves that make them excellent runners.
Yán Dì's grandson Bó Líng,
Bó Líng had relations with Wú Quán's wife Ā Nǚ Yuán Fù,
Yuán Fù was pregnant for three years,
and gave birth to Gǔ,
Yán, and Shū.
They first created targets,
Gǔ and Yán then first created bells,
and established musical styles.
Huángdì gave birth to Luòmíng,
Luòmíng gave birth to White Horse,
White Horse was Gǔn.
Dì Jùn gave birth to Yù Hào,
Yù Hào gave birth to Yín Liáng,
Yín Liáng gave birth to Pān Yú,
who first made boats.
Pān Yú gave birth to Xī Zhòng,
Xī Zhòng gave birth to Jí Guāng,
Jí Guāng was the first to use wood to make carts.
Shǎohào gave birth to Bān,
and Bān was the first to make bows and arrows.
Dì Jùn bestowed upon Yì a vermilion bow and white-shafted arrows,
to support the lower kingdoms.
Yì thus began to alleviate the myriad hardships of the lower lands.
Dì Jùn gave birth to Yàn Lóng,
Yàn Lóng became the inventor of the qín and sè.
Dì Jùn had eight sons,
who began to create songs and dances.
Dì Jùn gave birth to Sān Shēn,
Sān Shēn gave birth to Yì Jūn,
Yì Jūn was the first to become the skillful Chuí,
and was the first to create the various crafts for the common people.
Hòu Jì sowed the hundred grains.
The grandson of Jì was named Shū Jūn,
who was the first to initiate ox-drawn plowing.
Dà Bǐ Chì Yīn,
was the first to establish a state.
Yǔ and Gǔn were the first to distribute the soil,
evenly stabilizing the Nine Provinces.
Yán Dì's wife,
the daughter of Chì Shuǐ, Tīng Yāo, gave birth to Yán Jū.
Yán Jū gave birth to Jié Bìng.
Jié Bìng gave birth to Xì Qì.
Xì Qì gave birth to Zhù Róng.
Zhù Róng descended and dwelled by the Jiāng Shuǐ,
where he gave birth to Gòng Gōng.
Gòng Gōng gave birth to Shù Qì.
Shù Qì had a square head at the crown,
and he restored the fertile soil,
dwelling by the Jiāng Shuǐ.
Gòng Gōng gave birth to Hòu Tǔ.
Hòu Tǔ gave birth to Yē Míng.
Yē Míng gave birth to the twelve months of the year.
The floodwaters reached the heavens.
Gǔn stole the Dí’s Xìrǎng to block the floodwaters,
without awaiting the Dí’s command.
The Dí ordered Zhùróng to kill Gǔn at Yǔjiāo.
From Gǔn’s body, Yǔ was born.
The Dí then commanded Yǔ to finally spread the soil and stabilize the Nine Provinces.
